schema_notes.is_historical_867: True if the barony name is contemporarily attested as a settlement, fortress, or administrative unit by <= 867 CE.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: True if the barony name directly adopts a specific proper hydronym, oronym, choronym, or named topographic feature (excluding directional/locator compounds).
schema_notes.older_name_by_867: Records attested pre-867 CE names for the same site or immediate predecessor when distinct from the barony name.

b_MAL_Kedah.first_mention_attestation: 671 CE (recorded as Jiecha / Chieh-ch'a 羯荼 by the Chinese Buddhist pilgrim Yijing; later/related Indian forms include Sanskrit Kaṭāha and Tamil Kaṭāram / Kiḍāram in 11th-century CE Chola inscriptions, 1017–1025 CE, while the Sangam poem Paṭṭiṉappālai, c. 2nd century CE, uses Kāḻakam)

morphemes.translation: kettle, cauldron, or iron-smelting pan (or from Sanskrit khedda 'elephant trap')

b_MAL_Kedah.etymology_analysis: Malay 'Kedah' derives from early Indianized toponyms Sanskrit Kaṭāha ('cauldron/kettle') and Old Tamil Kaṭāram (often linked to ancient iron-smelting in the Sungai Batu/Bujang region), transcribed by Yijing in 671 CE as Jiecha (羯荼) and by Arab geographers as Kalah/Qataha.

b_MAL_Terang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; 'Terang' is the traditional Malay exonym for Trang (recorded in Kedah historical traditions prior to 1810 CE)

morphemes.translation: bright, clear (or Malay adaptation of Thai Trang)

b_MAL_Terang.etymology_analysis: In Malay historiography, 'Terang' refers to the northern border territory of Trang (ceded by Kedah to Siam in 1810 CE); folk etymology connects it to Malay terang ('bright, clear'), though it likely reflects a Malay phonological adaptation of Trang.

b_MAL_Bujang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE as a written toponym; the Bujang Valley archaeological complex dates from the 2nd–14th centuries CE, while the name 'Bujang' is a later Malay/Sanskrit-derived designation

morphemes.translation: serpent, dragon, or scholar/sage (via Malay bujang)

b_MAL_Bujang.etymology_analysis: Commonly derived from Sanskrit bhujaṅga ('serpent' or 'scholar', yielding 'Scholars' Valley' for Lembah Bujang), though in modern Malay bujang means 'unmarried/youth'; the name is not contemporarily attested in pre-867 CE inscriptions.

b_MAL_Bukit_Batu_Pahat.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; the 6th–7th century CE Hindu temple ruin at the site is known by the modern Malay descriptive name 'Bukit Batu Pahat'
b_MAL_Bukit_Batu_Pahat.etymology_analysis: Modern Malay descriptive toponym meaning 'Hill of Carved Stone', referring to the carved granite blocks of the Candi Bukit Batu Pahat Hindu temple complex in the Bujang Valley.

current_repo_state.name: Bukit Batu Pahat
current_repo_state.b_origin: Bukit Batu Pahat (constituent holding of Kedâh)

b_MAL_Kelantan.first_mention_attestation: 1225 CE (recorded as Ji-lan-tan / Kilan-tan 吉蘭丹 in Zhao Rugua's Zhu Fan Zhi; also Kalanten in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama)
b_MAL_Kelantan.etymology_analysis: Origin debated: proposed derivations include Malay kilatan ('place of lightning/flashes'), gelam hutan ('cajeput forest'), or Indian Kōlāntapuri; the name itself is first contemporarily attested in Song-era Chinese records (1225 CE) rather than <= 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Kelantan
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Kelantan).

b_MAL_Dungun.first_mention_attestation: 1365 CE (mentioned as Dhungun in Canto 14 of the Old Javanese Nagarakretagama)
b_MAL_Dungun.etymology_analysis: Named after the coastal mangrove tree pokok dungun (Heritiera littoralis) native to the Terengganu coast; first attested as Dhungun in the Nagarakretagama (1365 CE).

b_MAL_Tinggano.first_mention_attestation: 1225 CE (recorded as Deng-ya-nu / Tong-ya-nong 登牙儂 in Zhu Fan Zhi; later Tringgano in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama and Terengganu Inscription Stone of 1303 CE)
b_MAL_Tinggano.etymology_analysis: Variant/archaic spelling of Terengganu; folk etymology derives it from terang ganu ('bright rainbow') or taring anu ('tusk of something'). First contemporarily attested in Chinese records (1225 CE) and the Terengganu Inscription Stone (1303 CE).

b_MAL_Patani.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; 'Patani' / 'Pattani' emerges in the late medieval/early modern period (c. 15th–16th century CE) as the name of the Patani Sultanate
b_MAL_Patani.etymology_analysis: Local tradition derives Patani from Patani Malay pata ni ('this beach') or Pak Tani ('Father Tani'); another hypothesis links it to Sanskrit pathinī ('virgin nymph'). The pre-867 polity in this area was Langkasuka.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Liang Shu (Book of Liang), 515 CE embassy
older_name_by_867.notes: Langkasuka (Chinese Langyaxiu 狼牙脩) was centered in the Yarang/Pattani area and sent its first recorded embassy to China in 515 CE.

b_MAL_Saiburi.first_mention_attestation: 1938 CE (the district in Pattani was renamed Sai Buri in 1938 CE, having been called Mueang/Taluban earlier; note that Thai 'Sai Buri' also served as an exonym for Kedah)
b_MAL_Saiburi.etymology_analysis: Thai compound combining sai ('banyan' or adapted from Malay Sungai/Teluban) and buri (from Sanskrit purī, 'city/town'). Historically known in Malay as Teluban.

b_MAL_Menara.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; 'Menara' is the traditional Malay name for Narathiwat (renamed Bang Nara and then Narathiwat in 1915 CE)
b_MAL_Menara.etymology_analysis: Malay menara ('tower, minaret'), borrowed from Arabic manāra; the pre-Islamic name of the settlement is unknown, and it was later Thai-ized as Bang Nara before being renamed Narathiwat in 1915 CE.

b_THAI_Chaiya.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE under the Thai name 'Chaiya'; the site was a major Srivijayan center attested in the 775 CE Wat Sema Mueang / Ligor-Chaiya stele (naming Śrīvijaya) and later as Grahi in the 1183 CE Grahi inscription

morphemes.translation: victory (phonetic contraction of Śrīvijaya / Jaya, or from Malay cahaya 'light')

b_THAI_Chaiya.etymology_analysis: Thai Chaiya (ไชยา), historic Srivijayan and later Grahi center in Surat Thani Province, southern Thailand; widely derived either as a phonetic contraction of Sanskrit Śrīvijaya / Jaya ('victory') or from Malay cahaya ('light'). The 775 CE Ligor/Chaiya stele documents Srivijaya's royal shrines here.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Wat Sema Mueang / Ligor-Chaiya Inscription (697 Saka / 775 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: The 775 CE Sanskrit stele from Wat Hua Wiang / Wat Sema Mueang in the Chaiya area records a King of Śrīvijaya erecting three brick Buddhist shrines, establishing Chaiya as a major pre-867 Srivijayan outpost prior to its 1183 CE attestation as Grahi and later Thai name Chaiya.

b_THAI_Takua_Pa.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE under the Thai name 'Takua Pa'; the ancient trans-peninsular port at this site was attested as Takola in the 2nd century CE (and a 9th-century Tamil inscription at Takua Pa records the Manigramam guild and Avani-naranam tank)
b_THAI_Takua_Pa.etymology_analysis: Thai Takua Pa literally means 'lead/tin forest', reflecting the region's alluvial tin and lead deposits (or a Thai folk-etymological reshaping of ancient Takola).

older_name_by_867.notes: Takola / Takkola was an ancient port on the Kra Isthmus attested in Ptolemy (c. 150 CE), the Milinda Panha, and the 1030 CE Tanjore inscription (Talaittakkolam).

b_THAI_Ranang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; 'Ranang' is an archaic/Malay spelling of Ranong, a southern Thai tin-mining town that rose in the Rattanakosin era (19th century CE)

morphemes.translation: place name of uncertain origin (possibly from Malay renang 'swimming' or local kra/tin term)

b_THAI_Ranang.etymology_analysis: Variant/Malay spelling of Ranong on the Kra Isthmus; the settlement gained prominence in the 19th century CE under Governor Khaw Soo Cheang during the Rattanakosin period.

b_THAI_Gerbi.first_mention_attestation: 1872 CE (Krabi was elevated to town status by King Chulalongkorn in 1872 CE; 'Gerbi' is the older Malay/colonial rendering of Krabi)

morphemes.translation: sword (or monkey, preserving old banner symbolism)

b_THAI_Gerbi.etymology_analysis: 'Gerbi' is the traditional Malay and 19th-century European spelling of Krabi; in Thai, krabi means 'sword' (or 'monkey' from Sanskrit kapi), officially adopted when Krabi was elevated to town status in 1872 CE.

b_THAI_Ligor.first_mention_attestation: 1515 CE (recorded as Ligor in Tomé Pires' Suma Oriental, c. 1512–1515 CE, reflecting the Malay maritime exonym for Nakhon Si Thammarat / Nagara Sri Dharmaraja; the same site was attested earlier as Tambralinga from c. 200 CE)

morphemes.translation: city, royal capital (Malay/Portuguese adaptation of Thai Lakhon / Sanskrit Nagara Sri Dharmaraja)

b_THAI_Ligor.etymology_analysis: Historical Malay and European exonym for Nakhon Si Thammarat in southern Thailand, derived via Malay phonetic adaptation of Thai Lakhon (itself a shortening of Sanskrit Nagara in Nagara Sri Dharmaraja); documented in Portuguese records from c. 1512–1515 CE.

older_name_by_867.notes: The ancient Hindu-Buddhist kingdom centered at Nakhon Si Thammarat / Ligor was attested as Tambalinga in the Pali Niddesa (c. 200 CE), later as Danliumei in Song records (1001 CE) and Madamalingam in the 1030 CE Tanjore inscription.

b_THAI_Kanchanadit.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; the area was historically known as Tha Thong before being renamed Kanchanadit in the Rattanakosin era
b_THAI_Kanchanadit.etymology_analysis: Thai administrative name from Sanskrit kāñcana ('gold') + diś ('direction'), translating earlier Thai Tha Thong ('Golden Pier'); not attested before the modern/Rattanakosin era.

b_THAI_Mardelang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; 'Mardelang' (Mardelong) is the traditional Malay exonym for Phatthalung, which became a royal city of Ayutthaya in the 14th century CE
b_THAI_Mardelang.etymology_analysis: Malay historical exonym (Mardelong / Mardelang) for Phatthalung in southern Thailand, reflecting Malay-Muslim contact in the late medieval/early modern period.

b_THAI_Trang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE under the name 'Trang' (formerly Mueang Thap Thiang; Trang's association with Ptolemy's Takola is debated)

morphemes.translation: bright, clear (borrowed into Thai as Trang)

b_THAI_Trang.etymology_analysis: Named after the Trang River, commonly derived from Malay terang ('bright, clear'); while some scholars associate the coastal region with Ptolemy's Takola, the name Trang itself is not attested by 867 CE.

b_MAL_Beruas.first_mention_attestation: 1515 CE (attested as Bruas in Tomé Pires' Suma Oriental, c. 1512–1515 CE, and in the Sejarah Melayu / Malay Annals as a Malay riverine kingdom in Perak succeeding Gangga Negara)
b_MAL_Beruas.etymology_analysis: Named after the pokok beruas (seashore mangosteen, Garcinia hombroniana), a coastal tree native to Perak, Malaysia; historic Malay kingdom succeeding Gangga Negara and attested as Bruas by Tomé Pires (1512–1515 CE).

b_MAL_Kelang.first_mention_attestation: 1365 CE (recorded as Kelang in Canto 14 of the Old Javanese Nagarakretagama)
b_MAL_Kelang.etymology_analysis: Named after the Klang River; proposed etymologies include Mon-Khmer klong ('canal/waterway') or Malay kilang. First contemporarily attested as Kelang in the Nagarakretagama (1365 CE).

b_MAL_Sungei_Ujong.first_mention_attestation: 1365 CE (attested as Sanghyang Hujung in Canto 14 of the Old Javanese Nagarakretagama; modern Malay Sungei/Sungai Ujong)
b_MAL_Sungei_Ujong.etymology_analysis: Malay Sungai Ujong ('End River' or 'River's End'), corresponding to Sanghyang Hujung in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama; historically the old name of the Seremban region in Negeri Sembilan.

b_MAL_Gelanggi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; 'Kota Gelanggi' appears in the 17th-century Malay Annals (Sejarah Melayu) as a legendary city raided by Rajendra Chola I (1025 CE)

morphemes.translation: treasury of gems (associated with Ganggayu in Sejarah Melayu)

b_MAL_Gelanggi.etymology_analysis: Name of a limestone cave complex in Pahang and a legendary lost city in Johor mentioned in the Sejarah Melayu (often associated with Ganggayu, 'treasury of gems'); not contemporarily attested <= 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Gelanggi
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Gelanggi).

b_MAL_Muar.first_mention_attestation: 1365 CE (mentioned as Muwar in Canto 14 of the Old Javanese Nagarakretagama)

morphemes.translation: river mouth, estuary (or proposed Sanskrit muna-ar 'three rivers')

b_MAL_Muar.etymology_analysis: Named after the Muar River, generally derived from Malay muara ('river mouth/estuary'); first contemporarily attested as Muwar in the Nagarakretagama (1365 CE).

b_MAL_Endau.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; modern Malay coastal town and river name in northeastern Johor

morphemes.translation: proper river/place name of uncertain origin

b_MAL_Endau.etymology_analysis: Town at the mouth of the Endau River on the Johor-Pahang border; the toponym has no documented attestation <= 867 CE.

b_MAL_Kundur.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; refers to Kundur Island in the Riau Archipelago (or a local Malay place name)
b_MAL_Kundur.etymology_analysis: Malay kundur ('wax gourd'), naming Kundur Island in the Riau Archipelago; unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.

b_MAL_Tumasik.first_mention_attestation: 1349 CE (recorded as Danmaxi 淡馬錫 in Wang Dayuan's Daoyi Zhilüe; also Tumasik in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama)

morphemes.translation: lake, sea (with infix -um-/-em-, 'place surrounded by sea')

b_MAL_Tumasik.etymology_analysis: Old Malay Tumasik / Temasek, likely derived from tasik ('sea/lake') with the Austronesian infix -um-/-em- ('sea-town'); first contemporarily attested in 1349 CE (Daoyi Zhilüe) and 1365 CE (Nagarakretagama).

current_repo_state.name: Tumâsich
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Johor Sultanate was founded 1528 AD; resolves via Option A to ancestral maritime emporium Tumasik (Tumâsich).

b_MAL_Johor.first_mention_attestation: 1528 CE (founded as the Johor Sultanate in 1528 CE; earlier the area was known as Ujong Medini in 1365 CE and Ujong Tanah)
b_MAL_Johor.etymology_analysis: Derived from Arabic jauhar (borrowed from Persian gauhar, 'jewel/precious stone'), reflecting the gemstone trade along the Johor River; the name Johor postdates 867 CE and became prominent with the 1528 CE Johor Sultanate.

b_MAL_Penawar.first_mention_attestation: 1972 CE (Bandar Penawar was established in 1972 CE by KEJORA, named after nearby Tanjung Penawar)
b_MAL_Penawar.etymology_analysis: Modern planned town (Bandar Penawar, established 1972 CE) named after Cape Penawar (Tanjung Penawar); Malay penawar means 'antidote/remedy'.

b_MAL_Pekan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; 'Pekan' ('the town') emerged in the 15th–16th centuries CE as the vernacular Malay name for the royal capital of Pahang (earlier known in Sanskrit as Pura / Inderapura)

morphemes.translation: town, market town (vernacular equivalent of earlier Sanskrit Pura; also linked in local lore to bunga pekan, a white wild flower)

b_MAL_Pekan.etymology_analysis: Malay pekan ('town, marketplace'), originating as Pekan Pahang ('the town of Pahang') to replace the earlier Sanskrit court name Pura / Inderapura following Malaccan expansion in the 15th century CE; royal seat of Pahang.

current_repo_state.name: Pahang
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Pahang).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Song Shu (Book of Song), 449 CE embassy
older_name_by_867.notes: The lower Pahang polity around Pekan / Inderapura is identified by historians with Pohuang / Panhuang (婆皇) recorded in the Song Shu (449–450 CE), prior to the later Malay town name Pekan.

b_MAL_Inderapura.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; 'Inderapura' is recorded in later Malay historiography (Sejarah Melayu) as the pre-15th-century Sanskritic name of Pekan / Old Pahang
b_MAL_Inderapura.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Indrapura ('City of Indra'), the classical Hindu-Buddhist name for Pekan/Pahang in Malay tradition; while Old Pahang is attested from 449 CE as Pohuang, the specific name Inderapura is not attested <= 867 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Song Shu (Book of Song), 449 CE embassy
older_name_by_867.notes: Old Pahang (centered at Pekan/Inderapura) was attested in the Book of Song in 449–450 CE as Pohuang / Panhuang (婆皇).

b_MAL_Kiuli.first_mention_attestation: Unattested with certainty by 867 CE; proposed by some scholars to correspond to Kole polis in Ptolemy's Geographike Hyphegesis (c. 150 CE) on the northeast coast of the Golden Chersonese, though the localization and identification with Kiuli remain debated.
b_MAL_Kiuli.etymology_analysis: Reflects Ptolemy's Kole polis (Koli, c. 150 CE), a trading settlement placed by various scholars on the east coast of the Malay Peninsula (between Kelantan, Terengganu, and Kuantan in Pahang).

b_MAL_Saimwang.first_mention_attestation: 1365 CE (mentioned as Saimwang in Canto 14 of the Old Javanese Nagarakretagama)

morphemes.translation: ethnonym/toponym (associated with the Semang people or interior Malay Peninsula)

b_MAL_Saimwang.etymology_analysis: Recorded once in Canto 14 of the Nagarakretagama (1365 CE) alongside Langkasuka and Kelantan; scholars generally interpret Saimwang as referring to the Semang interior region of the Malay Peninsula.

b_MAL_Semantan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; modern Malay river and mukim name in Temerloh/Bentong, Pahang
b_MAL_Semantan.etymology_analysis: Named after the Semantan River (Sungai Semantan) in central Pahang; no pre-867 CE written attestation exists.

current_repo_state.name: Semantan
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Semantan).

b_MAL_Segamat.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; local tradition places the naming around 1511 CE during the fall of the Malacca Sultanate
b_MAL_Segamat.etymology_analysis: Named after the Segamat River; local folklore attributes the name to Malay segar amat ('very refreshing'), allegedly uttered by Bendahara Tepok of Malacca around 1511 CE.

b_riau.first_mention_attestation: 1719 CE (became prominent when Raja Kecil moved the Malay court to Ulu Riau in 1719 CE; possibly from 16th-century Portuguese rio 'river')
b_riau.etymology_analysis: Proposed etymologies include Portuguese rio ('river', 16th century CE), Malay riuh ('crowded/bustling'), or Arabic-Persian riyāḥī; the name is post-medieval and unattested <= 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Riau
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Riau).

b_siantan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Negeri Siantan (Anambas) appears in post-16th-century Malay and Bugis chronicles
b_siantan.etymology_analysis: Principal island of the Anambas Archipelago in the Riau Islands, sharing its name with the Malay bunga siantan (Ixora); unattested in pre-867 CE sources.

b_SUM_Lamuri.first_mention_attestation: 851 CE (recorded by Arab geographers from the 9th century CE onward, starting with Akhbar al-Sin wa-l-Hind in 851 CE as Rām(n)ī / Lāmurī; later Ilāmuridēśam in the 1030 CE Tanjore inscription)
b_SUM_Lamuri.etymology_analysis: Acehnese Lam Muri (with common Acehnese toponymic prefix lam- 'in/inside'), rendered by 9th-century CE Arab geographers as Rāmnī/Lāmurī, by Tamils as Ilāmuridēśam (1030 CE), and by Marco Polo as Lambri (1292 CE).

b_SUM_Barat.first_mention_attestation: 1365 CE (recorded as Barat in Canto 13 of the Old Javanese Nagarakretagama, denoting the west coast of Aceh)
b_SUM_Barat.etymology_analysis: Malay/Javanese directional term barat ('west'), referring to the western coast of Aceh in the Nagarakretagama (1365 CE).

b_SUM_Samudra.first_mention_attestation: 1267 CE (founded by Malikussaleh / Merah Silu in 1267 CE; attested in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama as Samudra)
b_SUM_Samudra.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit samudra ('ocean'), adopted as the capital name of the Samudera Pasai Sultanate founded in 1267 CE (and the etymological source of the island name Sumatra).

b_SUM_Pasai.first_mention_attestation: 1267 CE (paired with Samudera as the Samudera Pasai Sultanate founded in 1267 CE; Malikussaleh's tombstone at Pasai is dated 1297 CE)

morphemes.translation: settlement name (folk-etymologized as named after Merah Silu's hunting dog, Si Pasai)

b_SUM_Pasai.etymology_analysis: Acehnese Pase / Malay Pasai; according to the Hikayat Raja-raja Pasai, named after Sultan Malikussaleh's hunting dog Si Pasai in the late 13th century CE. Unattested <= 867 CE.

b_SUM_Panai.first_mention_attestation: 1030 CE (attested as Pannai in the Tanjore inscription of Rajendra Chola I; later Pane in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama)

morphemes.translation: river and kingdom name (proposed link to Tamil paṇṇai 'cultivated land/settlement')

b_SUM_Panai.etymology_analysis: Located along the Panai and Barumun rivers in North Sumatra; first attested in the 1030 CE Tanjore inscription as Pannai and in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama as Pane.

b_SUM_Kemang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; modern Indonesian/Malay settlement name

morphemes.translation: Mangifera kemanga (a wild mango-like fruit tree native to Sumatra)

b_SUM_Kemang.etymology_analysis: Derived from the native Sumatran fruit tree kemang (Mangifera kemanga); no pre-867 CE historical attestation.

b_SUM_Bahal.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Candi Bahal (Padang Lawas) dates to the 11th–13th centuries CE, named after the modern village of Bahal
b_SUM_Bahal.etymology_analysis: Village in Padang Lawas, North Sumatra, home to the 11th–13th century CE Vajrayana Buddhist Candi Bahal (Biaro Bahal) temple complex; unattested <= 867 CE.

b_SUM_Tanjung.first_mention_attestation: 1620 CE (Kampung Tanjung was established at the confluence of the Asahan and Silau rivers around 1620 CE, becoming Tanjungbalai)
b_SUM_Tanjung.etymology_analysis: Malay tanjung ('cape/promontory'), referring to Kampung Tanjung (later Tanjungbalai) at the mouth of the Asahan River, founded in the early 17th century CE.

b_SUM_Perlak.first_mention_attestation: 1292 CE (contemporarily attested by Marco Polo as Ferlec; later Parllak in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama; later Acehnese chronicles claim an 840 CE founding, which lacks contemporary corroboration)
b_SUM_Perlak.etymology_analysis: Named after the kayu peureulak timber tree native to eastern Aceh; while later Acehnese chronicles date the Peureulak Sultanate to 840 CE, its first contemporary attestation is Marco Polo's Ferlec (1292 CE).

b_SUM_Medan.first_mention_attestation: 1590 CE (founded on 1 July 1590 CE as Kampung Medan Putri by Guru Patimpus Sembiring Pelawi)

morphemes.translation: to recover/heal (Karo madan) or open field/square (Malay medan)

b_SUM_Medan.etymology_analysis: Founded in 1590 CE by Guru Patimpus; derived either from Karo Batak madan ('to be healed/better') or Malay medan ('open field/ground', from Arabic maydān).

b_SUM_Aru.first_mention_attestation: 1282 CE (first recorded in Yuan dynasty Chinese chronicles in 1282 CE; later Haru in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama)

morphemes.translation: kingdom name (proposed link to ethnonym Karo or coastal tree aru/ru)

b_SUM_Aru.etymology_analysis: Kingdom on the northeast coast of Sumatra (13th–16th centuries CE), possibly linked to the Karo ethnonym or the casuarina tree (ru/aru); first attested in Yuan Chinese records in 1282 CE.

b_SUM_Tamiang.first_mention_attestation: 1365 CE (attested as Tumihang in Canto 13 of the Old Javanese Nagarakretagama)

morphemes.translation: a type of bamboo (Schizostachyum blumei) or 'immune to bamboo itch'

b_SUM_Tamiang.etymology_analysis: Derived from buluh tamiang (bamboo) or Acehnese/Malay folk traditions regarding Raja Te-Miang; first contemporarily attested as Tumihang in the Nagarakretagama (1365 CE).

b_SUM_Dharmasraya.first_mention_attestation: 1286 CE (explicitly attested as Dharmāśraya in the 1208 Saka / 1286 CE Padang Roco inscription in West Sumatra under King Tribhuwanaraja Mauliwarmadewa; its Mauli dynasty is earlier attested in the 1183 CE Grahi inscription)
b_SUM_Dharmasraya.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Dharmāśraya ('abode/refuge of the Dharma'), capital of the medieval Melayu Kingdom under the Mauli dynasty in the upper Batanghari basin of West Sumatra, epigraphically attested in the 1286 CE Padang Roco inscription.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: New Book of Tang (644 CE embassy) and Yijing (671 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: The upper Batanghari basin of Dharmasraya lay within the historic Melayu Kingdom (Moluoyou 末羅瑜), attested in Tang records from 644 CE and Yijing in 671 CE.

b_SUM_Gudahiri.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources; 'Gudahiri' appears to be a non-historical or corrupted form (possibly a variant of Indragiri or Kuantan)
b_SUM_Gudahiri.etymology_analysis: Unattested in epigraphic, Chinese, Malay, or Dutch historical records; likely a corrupted or mod-coined toponym analogous to Indragiri.

b_SUM_Kuala_Kuantan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; modern Malay/Indonesian compound referring to the Kuantan River (Batang Kuantan) in Riau
b_SUM_Kuala_Kuantan.etymology_analysis: Malay kuala ('river mouth/confluence') + Kuantan (referring to the Batang Kuantan / upper Indragiri River in Riau); unattested <= 867 CE.

b_SUM_Indragiri.first_mention_attestation: Late 13th century CE (the Indragiri Kingdom was established in the late 13th century CE, later paying tribute to Malacca)
b_SUM_Indragiri.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Indragiri ('Mountain of Indra'), naming the Indragiri River and the late-13th-century Malay kingdom in Riau; unattested <= 867 CE.

b_SUM_Karitang.first_mention_attestation: 1365 CE (attested as Karitang in Canto 13 of the Old Javanese Nagarakretagama)

morphemes.translation: historic kingdom and riverine district in Indragiri Hilir

b_SUM_Karitang.etymology_analysis: Historically the Keritang Kingdom in Indragiri Hilir, Riau; first contemporarily attested as Karitang in the Nagarakretagama (1365 CE).

b_SUM_Rengat.first_mention_attestation: 1786 CE (founded as the capital of the Indragiri Sultanate by Sultan Ibrahim in 1786 CE)
b_SUM_Rengat.etymology_analysis: Town on the Indragiri River in Riau, founded in 1786 CE by Sultan Ibrahim of Indragiri; unattested <= 867 CE.

b_SUM_Jambi.first_mention_attestation: 852 CE (attested as Zhanbei / Chan-pei 占卑 sending embassies to Tang China in 852 and 871 CE; earlier the same region was recorded as Malayu / Moluoyou in 644 and 671 CE)

morphemes.translation: areca nut palm (Areca catechu, linked to Ratu Putri Selaras Pinang Masak)

b_SUM_Jambi.etymology_analysis: Derived from jambe ('areca nut palm') in local tradition; the name Jambi is contemporarily attested as Zhanbei (占卑) in Tang Chinese embassy records of 852 CE, succeeding the 7th-century name Malayu.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: New Book of Tang (644 CE embassy) and Yijing (671 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Prior to the 852 CE Zhanbei embassies, the Jambi polity was recorded as Moluoyou (末羅瑜, Malayu) in 644 CE and visited by Yijing in 671 CE.

b_SUM_Votabura.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources; 'Votabura' appears to be a non-historical or corrupted form
b_SUM_Votabura.etymology_analysis: Unattested in epigraphic, Chinese, Malay, or Indonesian historical sources; likely a mod-coined or corrupted pseudo-Sanskritic form ending in -bura/-pura.

b_SUM_Tungkal.first_mention_attestation: 1666 CE (attested during the Johor-Jambi War of 1666–1681 CE, when Tungkal came under Jambi Sultanate control)

morphemes.translation: river name / local coastal tree or stake

b_SUM_Tungkal.etymology_analysis: Named after the Tungkal River (centered at Kuala Tungkal in West Tanjung Jabung, Jambi); attested in 17th-century CE Johor-Jambi records, with no pre-867 CE attestation.

b_SUM_Tumbesi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before early modern Jambi Sultanate and Dutch colonial records of the Batang Tembesi river basin (17th–19th centuries CE).

morphemes.translation: Tembesi river name (locally associated with tembesu tree, Fagraea fragrans)

b_SUM_Tumbesi.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Batang Tembesi (Tembesi River), a major tributary of the Batang Hari in Jambi; local tradition links the name to the tembesu (Fagraea fragrans) hardwood tree.

b_SUM_Jamongas.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources prior to modern cartographic/modding usage as a constituent holding of Jambi.
b_SUM_Jamongas.etymology_analysis: No verified pre-modern attestation or established etymology in historical or epigraphic records of Jambi.

b_SUM_Karang_Brahi.first_mention_attestation: Modern Indonesian village name (Merangin, Jambi) where an Old Malay Śrīvijaya oath inscription dated c. 686 CE was discovered in 1904 CE; the inscription itself does not record the name Karang Brahi.

morphemes.translation: desire, passion (birahi), or local toponymic element

b_SUM_Karang_Brahi.etymology_analysis: Modern Malay toponym combining karang ('rock/outcrop') and brahi ('desire/passion', from birahi). While the site preserves a 686 CE Śrīvijaya oath inscription, the name Karang Brahi is a later vernacular designation.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Karang Brahi Old Malay inscription (c. 686 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: The 686 CE inscription at the site invokes the authority of Śrīvijaya without naming Karang Brahi.

b_SUM_Teba.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Teba in the Old Javanese Kakawin Nagarakretagama (1365 CE), Canto 13, listed among Sumatran territories of Malayu (identified with Muaro Tebo in upper Jambi).

morphemes.translation: riverbank clearing or Tebo river basin toponym

b_SUM_Teba.etymology_analysis: Old Javanese form Teba (modern Jambi Malay Tebo), corresponding to the Batang Tebo tributary of the Batang Hari in upper Jambi, listed in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama.

b_SUM_Lahat.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-modern written records; documented from the Dutch colonial period (19th century CE) in South Sumatra.

morphemes.translation: grave/niche or flat valley settlement toponym

b_SUM_Lahat.etymology_analysis: Vernacular South Sumatran Malay toponym for the highland town and regency along the Lematang River; while the surrounding Pasemah/Lahat area contains prehistoric megaliths, the name Lahat has no pre-867 CE attestation.

b_SUM_Lingga.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; appears in late medieval Malay and Chinese maritime records (14th–15th centuries CE, e.g., Ling-ya-men / Lingga Strait) and later as the center of the Riau-Lingga Sultanate.

morphemes.translation: emblem, pillar, or Mount Daik's three-pronged peak

b_SUM_Lingga.etymology_analysis: From Malay lingga (ultimately Sanskrit liṅga, 'emblem/pillar'), traditionally linked to the distinctive three-peaked silhouette of Mount Daik on Lingga Island.

b_SUM_Kampe.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Kampe in the Old Javanese Kakawin Nagarakretagama (1365 CE), Canto 13, among the Sumatran dependencies of Majapahit (also linked to Kampai / Kampai clan in eastern Sumatra).

morphemes.translation: Kampe / Kampai polity and clan toponym

b_SUM_Kampe.etymology_analysis: Old Javanese/Malay toponym attested in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama (Kampe), associated with the east Sumatran coastal polity of Kampai (Pulau Kampai) and the Malay Kampai clan.

b_SUM_Tanjungpinang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; the name Tanjungpinang emerged in the Johor–Riau Sultanate period (17th–18th centuries CE) on Bintan Island.
b_SUM_Tanjungpinang.etymology_analysis: Compound of Malay tanjung ('cape/promontory') and pinang ('areca nut palm'), referring to a prominent cape marked by areca palms at the mouth of the Bintan River.

b_SUM_Bengkulu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; documented from the early modern period (15th–17th centuries CE) and as British Bencoolen from 1685 CE.

morphemes.translation: riverbank or coast (also linked to bangkai, 'corpse', in folk etymology)

b_SUM_Bengkulu.etymology_analysis: Vernacular Malay toponym (anglicized as Bencoolen, Dutch Benkoelen), commonly explained from bang ('coast/riverbank') + hulu ('upstream') or local Rejang/Malay folk etymologies; unattested before the 15th–17th centuries CE.

b_SUM_Andalas.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; the name Andalas for Sumatra appears in post-13th-century CE Malay/Islamic geographic and literary tradition.

morphemes.translation: poetic/historical name for Sumatra (also linked to the andalas tree, Morus macroura)

b_SUM_Andalas.etymology_analysis: Post-13th-century CE literary/geographic name for the island of Sumatra, variously connected to the native andalas tree (Morus macroura) or Muslim travelers' comparison to Al-Andalus.

b_SUM_Padang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; Padang emerged as a documented coastal trading port in the 16th–17th centuries CE under Aceh and Dutch VOC influence.
b_SUM_Padang.etymology_analysis: From Minangkabau/Malay padang ('open field, plain'), describing the coastal lowland plain of West Sumatra.

b_SUM_Batan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources <= 867 CE; minor Minangkabau/West Sumatran constituent holding name.
b_SUM_Batan.etymology_analysis: Unattested in pre-modern epigraphy or chronicles; local West Sumatran toponymic holding.

b_SUM_Tiku.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Tiquo in Tomé Pires's Suma Oriental (c. 1515 CE) as a pepper-trading port on the west coast of Sumatra.

morphemes.translation: coastal settlement name in Agam, West Sumatra

b_SUM_Tiku.etymology_analysis: Minangkabau coastal toponym (Agam Regency, West Sumatra), attested from the early 16th century CE (Tomé Pires's Suma Oriental, c. 1515 CE) as a major pepper port.

b_SUM_Inderajati.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; appears only in post-medieval Minangkabau/Bengkulu coastal tradition.
b_SUM_Inderajati.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit-derived Malay compound of indera ('lord/king') and jati ('true/genuine'), paralleling nearby Inderapura and Indragiri; unattested <= 867 CE.

b_SUM_Muko_Muko.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; documented from the early modern period (17th–18th centuries CE) as a Minangkabau-linked coastal polity in northern Bengkulu.

morphemes.translation: front-most, facing, or coastal meeting point (reduplication of muko, 'face/front')

b_SUM_Muko_Muko.etymology_analysis: Reduplicated Minangkabau/Mukomuko form of muko ('face, front'), denoting a forward-facing coastal settlement on the Bengkulu–West Sumatra border.

current_repo_state.name: Muko Muko
current_repo_state.b_origin: Muko Muko (constituent holding of Rîach nan Berbedur)

b_SUM_Kota_Kapur.first_mention_attestation: Modern Indonesian village name on Bangka Island where the Old Malay Śrīvijaya inscription of 686 CE was discovered in 1892 CE; the inscription itself does not contain the name Kota Kapur.
b_SUM_Kota_Kapur.etymology_analysis: Malay compound of kota ('fort/town', from Sanskrit koṭṭa) and kapur ('lime/camphor'). Although the site yielded the 686 CE Kota Kapur inscription of Śrīvijaya, the name Kota Kapur itself is a later vernacular toponym.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Kota Kapur Old Malay inscription (686 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: The 686 CE inscription at the site invokes Śrīvijaya and curses disloyal subjects on Bangka without naming Kota Kapur.

b_SUM_Bangka.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by name <= 867 CE (the 686 CE Kota Kapur inscription on the island refers to Śrīvijaya and Bhūmi Jāva without naming Bangka); the island name appears in post-867 CE Malay, Javanese, and Chinese sources.

morphemes.translation: old, rigid, or tin-bearing island toponym (traditionally linked to wangka, 'tin')

b_SUM_Bangka.etymology_analysis: Island name in southeastern Sumatra, traditionally associated with wangka ('tin' in local/literary tradition) or Malay bangka; while settled and inscribed by Śrīvijaya in 686 CE, the name Bangka is not attested in 7th–9th century CE epigraphy.

b_SUM_Belitung.first_mention_attestation: Earliest written record of Belitung (as Ko-lan / Billiton) appears in the Yuan Shi's account of the 1292–1293 CE Mongol-Java expedition, followed by Yingya/Xingcha Shenglan (1436 CE).
b_SUM_Belitung.etymology_analysis: Malay/Belitung island name (historically anglicized/Dutch Billiton). Although a 9th-century CE Arabian dhow wreck (c. 826 CE) was found off its coast in 1998 CE, the island's name itself is unattested <= 867 CE.

b_SUM_Mesuji.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; modern district and river name on the South Sumatra–Lampung border.
b_SUM_Mesuji.etymology_analysis: Named after the Mesuji River flowing between South Sumatra (Ogan Komering Ilir) and Lampung; no pre-867 CE written attestation exists.

current_repo_state.name: Mesûdschi
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: East Sumatra is a modern English geographic descriptor; resolves via Option A to indigenous river district Mesuji (Mesûdschi).

b_SUM_FIC_Rawatimur.first_mention_attestation: Fictional/constructed holding name (marked FIC in repository key) with no historical attestation.
b_SUM_FIC_Rawatimur.etymology_analysis: Constructed Indonesian compound of rawa ('swamp/marsh') and timur ('east'), meaning 'eastern marshland', created as a fictional holding in eastern Sumatra.

b_SUM_Tulangbawang.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Tang-era Chinese histories and encyclopedias (such as Tongdian and Xin Tangshu, covering 7th-century CE embassies, c. 671 CE) as To-lang-po-hwang (Duōlángpóhuáng, 多郎婆黃), debated between the Tulang Bawang polity in Lampung, Sumatra and Java.
b_SUM_Tulangbawang.etymology_analysis: Identified by scholars (e.g., Gabriel Ferrand) with To-lang-po-hwang in 7th-century CE Chinese Buddhist/Tang records; literally 'onion bone' in Malay/Lampung, likely a folk-etymological rendering of an older indigenous hydronym.

b_SUM_Menggala.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; documented as an important pepper-trading river port on the Tulang Bawang River during the Banten Sultanate and Dutch colonial era (17th–19th centuries CE).

morphemes.translation: auspicious, fortunate, or local town name

b_SUM_Menggala.etymology_analysis: Historic port town on the Tulang Bawang River in Lampung; the name resembles Sanskrit maṅgala ('auspicious'), though the settlement name itself is unattested <= 867 CE.

b_SUM_Palas_Pasemah.first_mention_attestation: Modern village name in South Lampung where an undated late-7th-century CE (c. 686 CE) Old Malay Śrīvijaya oath inscription was found in 1956 CE; the inscription does not mention Palas Pasemah.
b_SUM_Palas_Pasemah.etymology_analysis: Modern village toponym combining palas (fan palm) and Pasemah (the South Sumatran highland group). Although a late-7th-century CE Śrīvijaya inscription was unearthed here, the village name is modern/post-867 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Palas Pasemah Old Malay inscription (late 7th century CE, c. 686 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: The late-7th-century CE inscription found at the site refers to Śrīvijaya rather than Palas Pasemah.

b_SUM_Batu_Betil.first_mention_attestation: Modern Indonesian archaeological site name in Tanggamus, Lampung, housing megaliths and a damaged Buddhist mantra inscription palaeographically dated to the 10th century CE.

morphemes.translation: gun, cannon (referring to cannon-shaped megalithic stones)

b_SUM_Batu_Betil.etymology_analysis: Malay compound of batu ('stone') and bedil ('cannon/gun'), named by locals after the elongated megalithic stones at the site; its Buddhist inscription dates to the 10th century CE, post-867 CE.

b_SUM_Pugong.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; modern village and archaeological park name (Pugung Raharjo) in East Lampung, preserving prehistoric/megalithic stepped pyramids and Hindu-Buddhist remains.
b_SUM_Pugong.etymology_analysis: Vernacular Lampung toponym associated with the traditional polity of Keratuan Pugung and the Pugung Raharjo megalithic site; unattested in written records <= 867 CE.

b_SUM_Palembang.first_mention_attestation: The name Palembang is first attested in Chinese as Pa-lin-fong (巴林馮) in Zhao Rugua's Zhu Fan Zhi (1225 CE) and in Javanese as Palembang in the Nagarakretagama (1365 CE); earlier 7th-century CE inscriptions at the site name Śrīvijaya and Matajap.

morphemes.translation: low-lying inundated land, or limbang ('panning gold')

b_SUM_Palembang.etymology_analysis: Formed with Malay locative prefix pe-/pa- + lembang ('inundated/waterlogged ground') or limbang ('to pan gold/ores'). While Palembang was the capital of Śrīvijaya from at least 682 CE, the toponym Palembang itself is post-867 CE.

older_name_by_867.notes: The 682 CE Kedukan Bukit inscription found in Palembang records the founding of Śrīvijaya (and mentions Matajap, identified with Mukha Upang in Palembang).

b_SUM_Minanga_Tamwan.first_mention_attestation: Contemporarily attested as Minānga Tamwan in the Old Malay Kedukan Bukit inscription (16 June 682 CE), as the river-confluence departure point of Dapunta Hyang Śrī Jayanāśa's expedition.
b_SUM_Minanga_Tamwan.etymology_analysis: Old Malay toponym meaning 'estuary/river junction' (minānga + tamwan, cognate with modern Malay temuan), attested in the 682 CE Kedukan Bukit inscription; scholars debate its location between the Komering, Musi, and Kampar river confluences.

b_SUM_Baros.first_mention_attestation: Portuguese/Malay spelling variant 'Baros' recorded in Tomé Pires's Suma Oriental (c. 1515 CE) for the ancient Sumatran camphor port of Barus.
b_SUM_Baros.etymology_analysis: Early modern Portuguese/Malay spelling variant of Barus (famous for camphor, kapur barus), placed in Palembang in the game repository; the underlying toponym Barus/Barousai is attested from c. 150 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Claudius Ptolemy, Geographia (c. 150 CE, Barousai) and 9th-century CE Arab geographers (Bālūs)
older_name_by_867.notes: The ancient port of Barus is attested as Barousai in Ptolemy (c. 150 CE) and Bālūs in 9th-century CE Arab geography prior to the Portuguese/Malay variant Baros (c. 1515 CE).

b_SUM_Salekar.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources prior to modern repository/gazetteer usage as a constituent holding of Palembang.
b_SUM_Salekar.etymology_analysis: No verified historical attestation or established etymology in South Sumatran epigraphy or chronicles.

b_SUM_Musi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; the hydronym Musi appears in later post-Srivijaya Malay and colonial records of South Sumatra.

morphemes.translation: proper name of Sumatra's major southern river

b_SUM_Musi.etymology_analysis: Named after the Musi River (Sungai Musi) of South Sumatra; although Palembang on its banks was attested in 682 CE, the river name Musi itself is not recorded in 7th-century CE Srivijayan inscriptions.

b_SUM_Batu_Brak.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; modern district and prehistoric megalithic site name in West Lampung associated with the Sekala Brak tradition.

morphemes.translation: wide, broad, or Sekala Brak ('broad/open plateau')

b_SUM_Batu_Brak.etymology_analysis: Lampung compound of batu ('stone') and brak ('broad/wide', shared with Sekala Brak), referring to the megalithic stone complexes of West Lampung.

b_SUM_Tanah_Abang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; modern district name in Penukal Abab Lematang Ilir (PALI), South Sumatra, containing the 9th–13th century CE Hindu-Buddhist Candi Bumiayu complex.

morphemes.translation: red (referring to red laterite soil or brick ruins)

b_SUM_Tanah_Abang.etymology_analysis: Malay/Javanese compound meaning 'red earth' (tanah + abang), likely reflecting the red brick temple ruins of Candi Bumiayu or local soil; unattested <= 867 CE.

b_SUM_Pedamaran.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; modern wetland district in Ogan Komering Ilir Regency, South Sumatra.
b_SUM_Pedamaran.etymology_analysis: Malay locative formation pe-damar-an ('place of damar resin'), referring to a traditional resin-producing or trading settlement in the Komering floodplain.

b_SUM_Kampar.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Kampar in the Old Javanese Kakawin Nagarakretagama (1365 CE), Canto 13, listed among the Sumatran dependencies of Majapahit.

morphemes.translation: river and region name in central-eastern Sumatra

b_SUM_Kampar.etymology_analysis: Toponym and hydronym of the Kampar River basin in Riau, first attested in writing in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama (earlier associated with the Srivijayan temple complex of Muara Takus).

b_SUM_Siak.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Siak in the Old Javanese Kakawin Nagarakretagama (1365 CE), Canto 13, among Majapahit's Sumatran dependencies (later seat of the Sultanate of Siak Sri Indrapura, 1723 CE).

morphemes.translation: river and polity name (also associated with the siak-siak plant, Dianella ensifolia)

b_SUM_Siak.etymology_analysis: Hydronym and polity name of eastern Riau, first attested in 1365 CE in the Nagarakretagama; local tradition derives it from the siak-siak plant growing along the Siak River.

b_SUM_Boron.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources prior to modern repository usage as a constituent holding of Kampar.
b_SUM_Boron.etymology_analysis: No verified pre-modern attestation or established etymology in Riau historical records.

b_SUM_Suir.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; documented in modern Riau records as the Suir River (Sungai Suir) on Tebing Tinggi Island in Meranti Islands Regency.

morphemes.translation: local river name on Tebing Tinggi Island

b_SUM_Suir.etymology_analysis: Named after the Suir River (Sungai Suir) on Tebing Tinggi Island in the Meranti Islands, Riau; unattested <= 867 CE.

b_SUM_Selat_Panjang.first_mention_attestation: Founded/renamed Selat Panjang in the late 19th to early 20th century CE (previously Bandar Tebing Tinggi, renamed under Siak administration prior to 1908 CE).
b_SUM_Selat_Panjang.etymology_analysis: Malay compound meaning 'long strait' (selat + panjang), referring to the long narrow channel between Tebing Tinggi, Padang, and Rangsang islands in Riau.

b_SUM_Muara_Takus.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in writing in 1860 CE by Dutch researcher Cornets de Groot; the Buddhist temple complex itself dates to the Srivijayan period (c. 11th–12th centuries CE, with some estimates earlier), without contemporary epigraphic attestation of the name Muara Takus.
b_SUM_Muara_Takus.etymology_analysis: Malay compound of muara ('river mouth/confluence') and Takus (the local Takus River joining the Kampar Kanan). The temple complex is Srivijayan, but the modern name Muara Takus is unattested <= 867 CE.

b_SUM_Pagaruyung.first_mention_attestation: Established as the royal seat of Ādityavarman in 1347 CE (Pagaruyung/Amoghapāśa inscriptions of 1347 CE onward in Tanah Datar, West Sumatra).

morphemes.translation: hard outer wood of the sugar palm (Arenga pinnata)

b_SUM_Pagaruyung.etymology_analysis: Minangkabau/Malay compound of pagar ('fence/palisade') and ruyung ('sugar palm timber'), referring to a settlement palisaded with palm wood; founded as a kingdom in 1347 CE.

b_SUM_Kahwas.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Kahwas in the Old Javanese Kakawin Nagarakretagama (1365 CE), Canto 13, listed beside Kandis in central Sumatra.

morphemes.translation: central Sumatran polity toponym (identified with Kawas/Kawai)

b_SUM_Kahwas.etymology_analysis: Old Javanese transcription of a central Sumatran (Minangkabau/Riau) polity name (variously identified with Kawas or Kawai), attested in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama.

b_SUM_Kuntu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; known in Riau historiography as the medieval polity of Kuntu-Kampar (12th–14th centuries CE, attacked by Ādityavarman in the 14th century CE).

morphemes.translation: traditional Kampar Kiri settlement and polity name

b_SUM_Kuntu.etymology_analysis: Traditional Kampar Kiri toponym in Riau, historically significant as an early Islamic trading center (Kuntu-Kampar) in the post-867 CE medieval period.

b_SUM_Pekanbaru.first_mention_attestation: Named Pekanbaru ('new market') in 1784 CE (23 June 1784 CE, celebrated as its founding date) when Sultan Muhammad Ali Abdul Jalil Muazzam Syah of Siak relocated the market of Senapelan.
b_SUM_Pekanbaru.etymology_analysis: Malay compound of pekan ('market') and baru ('new'), literally 'New Market', coined in 1784 CE to replace the earlier 17th-century CE settlement name Senapelan.

current_repo_state.name: Nider-Rôkan
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Pekanbaru ('New Market') was founded in 1784 AD; resolves via Option A to lower Rokan river district (Nider-Rôkan).

b_SUM_Rokan_Hilir.first_mention_attestation: Modern Indonesian administrative regency name created on 4 October 1999 CE from Bengkalis Regency (incorporating the lower Rokan River basin).
b_SUM_Rokan_Hilir.etymology_analysis: Modern Indonesian administrative compound combining the Rokan River name with hilir ('downstream'), formed in 1999 CE.

b_SUM_Rokan.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Rokan in the Old Javanese Kakawin Nagarakretagama (1365 CE), Canto 13, listed among the Sumatran dependencies of Majapahit.

morphemes.translation: Rokan River and medieval kingdom name

b_SUM_Rokan.etymology_analysis: Hydronym and polity name of the Rokan River basin in northern Riau, first attested in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama.

b_SUM_Bengkalis.first_mention_attestation: Documented in early 18th-century CE Malay/Siak history (1717 CE, when Raja Kecil assembled forces at Bengkalis before founding the Siak Sultanate in 1723 CE).

morphemes.translation: island name (folk etymology from mengkal, 'sad/unripe', + kalis, 'steadfast')

b_SUM_Bengkalis.etymology_analysis: Island and regency name off eastern Sumatra in the Strait of Malacca; local folk etymology derives it from Raja Kecil's expression mengkal tetapi kalis ('grieved yet steadfast'), though it is unattested <= 867 CE.

b_SUM_Kalowang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources prior to modern repository usage as a constituent holding of Rokan.
b_SUM_Kalowang.etymology_analysis: Resembles Malay/Indonesian kaluang/kalowang ('flying fox bat'), though no pre-modern Sumatran settlement of this name is attested in historical records.

b_marakele.first_mention_attestation: Recorded in 20th-century CE ethnography (A. R. Radcliffe-Brown, The Andaman Islanders, 1922 CE) as the Great Andamanese indigenous name for the Andaman archipelago.
b_marakele.etymology_analysis: Great Andamanese endonym meaning 'our homeland' or the Andaman archipelago, documented in early 20th-century CE ethnography; classical and medieval external sources instead used Angademan/Andaman.

older_name_by_867.notes: Ptolemy (2nd century CE) recorded the Andaman Islands as Angademan / Agathou Daimonos prior to 20th-century CE documentation of Marakele.

b_onge.first_mention_attestation: First documented by British colonial expeditions and ethnographers in the late 19th century CE (1867 CE Andaman Islands expedition and M. V. Portman in the 1880s–1890s CE).
b_onge.etymology_analysis: Endonym of the indigenous Onge (Önge) people of Little Andaman Island, meaning 'person/man' in the Ongan language; unattested in written records <= 867 CE.

b_diglipur.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; modern Indian-era town name in North Andaman Island (the site was briefly settled by the British as Port Cornwallis in 1792–1796 CE).
b_diglipur.etymology_analysis: Modern settlement name on North Andaman Island incorporating the Indo-Aryan suffix -pur ('town/city', from Sanskrit pura), established after post-independence settlement; unattested <= 867 CE.

b_nias.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Niyān (نيان) in Sulaiman al-Tajir's Arabic travelogue Akhbar al-Sin wa-l-Hind (851 CE), describing its coconut cultivation and headhunting customs.

morphemes.translation: human, person (endonym Tanö Niha, 'land of humans')

b_nias.etymology_analysis: Exonymic adaptation of Nias niha ('human', from Tanö Niha, 'land of humans'), attested in Arabic as Niyān by 851 CE.

b_simeulue.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; documented in Acehnese and Dutch colonial sources (17th–19th centuries CE) as Simeulue / Simalur.

morphemes.translation: island off northwestern Sumatra (also called Pulau Babi in early colonial maps)

b_simeulue.etymology_analysis: Indigenous/Acehnese island name off the western coast of Aceh; unattested in written sources <= 867 CE.

b_SUM_Barus.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Barousai (Βαροῦσαι) in Claudius Ptolemy's Geographia (c. 150 CE), later as Bālūs/Fansur in 9th-century CE Arab geography and in the 1088 CE Tamil Lobu Tuo inscription.
b_SUM_Barus.etymology_analysis: Ancient west Sumatran port renowned across the Indian Ocean for camphor (Malay kapur barus), attested in Greek as Barousai (c. 150 CE) and Arabic as Bālūs.

b_SUM_Singkil.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; documented in Acehnese and Dutch sources from the Aceh Sultanate period (16th–19th centuries CE).

morphemes.translation: coastal port and ethnic/linguistic region of southern Aceh

b_SUM_Singkil.etymology_analysis: Toponym of the coastal port and Batak-related Singkil people in southern Aceh; unattested in written records <= 867 CE.

b_SUM_Tripa.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; modern Acehnese river and peatland name (Sungai Tripa / Rawa Tripa) in Nagan Raya Regency.

morphemes.translation: river and peat swamp name on Aceh's west coast

b_SUM_Tripa.etymology_analysis: Named after the Tripa River (Krueng/Sungai Tripa) and Tripa peatland on the western coast of Aceh; unattested <= 867 CE.

b_SUM_Calang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; documented from the Dutch colonial period (early 20th century CE, Onderafdeeling Tjalang) as a coastal town in Aceh Jaya.

morphemes.translation: coastal town name in Aceh Jaya (colonial spelling Tjalang)

b_SUM_Calang.etymology_analysis: Acehnese coastal town name (spelled Tjalang in Dutch colonial administration); unattested in historical records <= 867 CE.

b_siberut.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; the Mentawai Islands first entered European written records upon Dutch contact in 1621 CE, with Siberut documented in the colonial era.

morphemes.translation: largest island of the Mentawai archipelago

b_siberut.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Mentawai name for the largest island of the Mentawai chain off West Sumatra; while inhabited since prehistory, the island name has no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_sipura.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary pre-867 CE written attestation; the Mentawai Islands first entered European records in 1621 CE, with Sipura/Sipora documented in later colonial surveys.

morphemes.translation: indigenous island name (etymology unrecorded in academic literature)

b_sipura.etymology_analysis: Sipura (officially Sipora) is the indigenous Mentawai name for the central island of the Mentawai archipelago off western Sumatra. No pre-colonial written attestation of the island's name exists.

b_batu.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary pre-867 CE written attestation; the Batu Islands are documented in post-16th-century Malay and Dutch colonial records.
b_batu.etymology_analysis: From Malay and Indonesian 'batu' ('rock' or 'stone'), referring to the rocky archipelago located off the west coast of Sumatra between Nias and Siberut.

b_nakkavaram.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Nakkavaram' in the Tanjore (Thanjavur) Tamil inscription of Rajendra Chola I (1025–1030 CE).
b_nakkavaram.etymology_analysis: Tamil 'Nakkavaram' ('land of the naked'), recorded in Rajendra Chola I's 11th-century CE Tanjore inscription. It later evolved into the European colonial name 'Nicobar'.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Yijing (671–695 CE) as Lo-jen-kuo ('Country of the Naked'); Akhbar al-Sin wa-l-Hind (851 CE) as Lanjabalus
older_name_by_867.notes: Earlier Chinese and Arabic exonyms for the Nicobar Islands predating the 11th-century CE Tamil name Nakkavaram.

b_muot.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation; 'Muot' (Mūöt) is the indigenous Central Nicobarese endonym for Nancowry Island, documented in modern linguistic fieldwork.
b_muot.etymology_analysis: Mūöt (anglicized as Muot) is the indigenous Austroasiatic endonym for Nancowry Island and its Central Nicobarese language in the Nicobar Islands.

b_BOR_Brunei.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Barune' / 'Buruneng' in the Old Javanese Nagarakretagama (1365 CE, Canto 14.1).

morphemes.translation: sea god / seafarers (proposed etymon for Barunai/Brunei)

b_BOR_Brunei.etymology_analysis: The name 'Brunei' (14th-century 'Barunai' / 'Buruneng') is scholarly linked to Sanskrit 'varuṇa' (referring to seafarers or the sea), which also gave rise to the island name 'Borneo'. Local legend derives it from the Malay exclamation 'Baru nah!' ('There it is!'). Earlier Chinese 'Po-ni' (977 CE) postdates 867 CE.

b_BOR_Papar.first_mention_attestation: Documented in the 1877 CE Brunei concession to Alfred Dent and Baron von Overbeck; no pre-867 CE attestation.
b_BOR_Papar.etymology_analysis: From the Brunei Malay word 'papar', meaning 'flat land' ('tanah rata'), describing the coastal alluvial plain south of Kota Kinabalu in Sabah.

b_BOR_Seria.first_mention_attestation: Named after the Seria River following the 1929 CE oil discovery at Padang Berawa; no pre-867 CE attestation.

morphemes.translation: name of the local river (Sungai Seria)

b_BOR_Seria.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Seria River (Sungai Seria) in Belait District, Brunei. The area was formerly known locally as Padang Berawa ('Wild Pigeon's Field') before oil was struck in 1929 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Serîje
current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient Seria River basin of northern Borneo (in-game: Seria)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: 1929 oil town fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; resolved to ancient Seria river hydronym.

b_BOR_Punan.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary pre-867 CE written attestation; 'Punan' is an ethnographic exonym/ethnonym documented in 19th–20th century CE Borneo literature.

morphemes.translation: forest-dwelling interior hunter-gatherer groups of Borneo

b_BOR_Punan.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym referring to various interior forest-dwelling and riverine groups of Borneo (distinct from the Penan, though sometimes conflated in older literature). No pre-867 CE written record exists.

b_BOR_Kudat.first_mention_attestation: Founded as the first capital of British North Borneo on 7 December 1881 CE; previously known locally as Tomborungan / Tanjong Berungus.

morphemes.translation: colonial port name (earlier area called Tomborungan)

b_BOR_Kudat.etymology_analysis: Kudat was established in 1881 CE by the British North Borneo Company; the area was originally called Tomborungan by the indigenous Rungus people after the Tomborungus River.

current_repo_state.name: Marûdu
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Kudat was founded in 1881 by the British North Borneo Company; resolves via Option A to ancient Marudu Bay (Marûdu).

b_BOR_Marudu.first_mention_attestation: First mapped as 'Marudu' by a Dutch sailor in 1595 CE; no pre-867 CE written attestation.

morphemes.translation: a position located in the same place

b_BOR_Marudu.etymology_analysis: From Balangigi (Sama-Bajau) 'mairudu' or 'maiuludu' ('a position located in the same place'), referring to the geography of Marudu Bay in northern Sabah.

b_BOR_Kinabatangan.first_mention_attestation: Associated in Brunei and Sabah oral/historical traditions with 15th-century CE Chinese trade settlements; no contemporary pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_BOR_Kinabatangan.etymology_analysis: Widely explained as a contraction of 'Cina batangan' ('Chinese river/estuary'), reflecting early Chinese trading settlements along Malaysia's second-longest river, or locally 'sungai yang panjang' ('the long river').

b_BOR_Ranau.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary pre-867 CE written attestation; documented during British North Borneo colonial administration (late 19th–20th century CE).
b_BOR_Ranau.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Dusun word 'ranahon', meaning 'wet rice field' or 'paddy field', referring to the fertile highland valley in Sabah.

b_BOR_Lahad_Datu.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE attestation; the name arose from the migration of Sulu datus after the 17th-century CE Brunei Civil War, and the district was organized under British North Borneo (post-1878 CE).
b_BOR_Lahad_Datu.etymology_analysis: From Bajau 'lahad' ('place') and 'datu' ('noble title/chief'), commemorating the settlement of Sulu datus led by Datu Puti after Brunei ceded eastern Sabah to Sulu.

current_repo_state.name: Sibûtu
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Lahad Datu is a 19th-c. town; resolves via Option A to ancient maritime strait Sibutu (Sibûtu).

b_BOR_Tawau.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned as a small fishing settlement (Tawao) in late 19th-century CE records following the 1878 CE Sulu concession and British North Borneo settlement in the 1890s CE.
b_BOR_Tawau.etymology_analysis: Earlier spelled 'Tawao', the town grew from a small late-19th-century CE fishing village into a British North Borneo port in the 1890s CE; its underlying etymology is uncertain.

b_BOR_Sibutu.first_mention_attestation: Specifically named in the 1900 CE Treaty of Washington (correcting its omission from the 1898 CE Treaty of Paris); no pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_BOR_Sibutu.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Sama-Bajau name for Sibutu Island and the Sibutu Strait between Sabah and Tawi-Tawi. No pre-867 CE written attestation exists.

b_BOR_Tarakan.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary pre-867 CE written attestation; documented in colonial-era Dutch and Tidung records (with oil exploration beginning in the late 19th/early 20th century CE).
b_BOR_Tarakan.etymology_analysis: According to Tidung tradition, 'Tarakan' combines 'tarak' ('meeting place') and 'ngakan' ('to eat'), referring to the island as a resting and dining stop for Tidung sailors and traders.

current_repo_state.name: Mendschelutung
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Mendschelutung).

b_BOR_Kadazan.first_mention_attestation: The ethnonym 'Kadazan' entered official censuses in Sabah in 1970 CE (following political adoption in the 1950s–1960s CE); no pre-867 CE attestation.
b_BOR_Kadazan.etymology_analysis: Commonly derived from 'kakadazan' ('towns') or 'kedai' ('shops'), referring to the coastal/urbanized Dusunic communities of Penampang and Papar in Sabah.

b_BOR_Dusun.first_mention_attestation: First described in European records by Thomas Forrest in 1774 CE as an exonym used by Bruneian Malay tax collectors; no pre-867 CE attestation.
b_BOR_Dusun.etymology_analysis: From Malay 'dusun' ('orchard'), part of the Bruneian Malay exonym 'Orang Dusun' ('orchard people') applied to the agricultural indigenous populations of northern Borneo.

current_repo_state.name: Nabâwan
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Nabâwan).

b_BOR_Selamban.first_mention_attestation: Known from Tidung oral history as the original settlement on the site of modern Malinau prior to Dutch colonial mapping; no pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_BOR_Selamban.etymology_analysis: Selamban was the pre-colonial Tidung settlement that preceded the Dutch-recorded name Malinau in North Kalimantan.

b_BOR_Tapean.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary pre-867 CE written attestation; 'Tapean' (Malay/Berau 'tapian'/'tepian') is a vernacular riverside term.
b_BOR_Tapean.etymology_analysis: Related to Malay/Berau 'tapian' or 'tepian' ('riverbank' or 'riverside landing place'), a common Bornean toponymic element without pre-867 CE attestation.

current_repo_state.name: Berau
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Berau).

b_BOR_Sambiliong.first_mention_attestation: Established as the Sultanate of Sambaliung in the early 19th century CE (following the division of the Berau Sultanate); no pre-867 CE attestation.

morphemes.translation: sultanate and district name in Berau

b_BOR_Sambiliong.etymology_analysis: Sambaliung (rendered 'Sambiliong' in the mod key) was one of the two successor sultanates (alongside Gunung Tabur) formed from the division of the Berau Sultanate in the early 19th century CE.

b_BOR_Tanjung_Selor.first_mention_attestation: Formally split from Tanjung Palas District in 2002 CE (and designated capital of North Kalimantan in 2012 CE); no pre-867 CE attestation.
b_BOR_Tanjung_Selor.etymology_analysis: Combines Malay 'tanjung' ('cape' or 'river bend') with 'Selor'. Located across the Kayan River from Tanjung Palas, the historic seat of the Bulungan Sultanate.

b_BOR_Badak.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation; Muara Badak is a modern coastal oil-and-gas district in Kutai Kartanegara.
b_BOR_Badak.etymology_analysis: From Malay/Indonesian 'badak' ('rhinoceros'), referring to the Muara Badak coastal area in East Kalimantan.

current_repo_state.name: Ferne-Kutai
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Post-867 Malay/Dayak directional subdivision ('Distant Kutai'); Procedure 2 confirms unbroken Dayak continuity, calquing jauh ('far') to Ferne-Kutai parallel to Nord-Kutai.

b_BOR_Melak.first_mention_attestation: Documented in Dutch colonial records by the 1930s CE (e.g., 1936 CE airfield planning near Melak); no pre-867 CE written attestation.

morphemes.translation: riverine settlement name on the upper Mahakam

b_BOR_Melak.etymology_analysis: Melak is a riverine town on the upper Mahakam River in West Kutai Regency, East Kalimantan, without pre-867 CE written attestation.

current_repo_state.name: Mahakâm
current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient pre-867 Mahakam River basin in Borneo (in-game: Melak)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Late river trading post fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; resolved to ancient Mahakam river basin.

b_BOR_Sangkulirang.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary pre-867 CE written attestation for the toponym 'Sangkulirang', though the nearby Sangkulirang-Mangkalihat karst caves contain prehistoric rock art.

morphemes.translation: bay and peninsula name in East Kutai

b_BOR_Sangkulirang.etymology_analysis: Sangkulirang designates the bay, karst region, and coastal district in East Kutai Regency, East Kalimantan. While prehistoric cave art exists in the karst, the name itself has no pre-867 CE written record.

current_repo_state.name: Nord-Kutai
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Nord-Kutai).

b_BOR_Sangkira.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation; likely a variant or adaptation of Sangkima in East Kutai, East Kalimantan.
b_BOR_Sangkira.etymology_analysis: No historical attestation exists for 'Sangkira' in East Kutai; it may represent a cartographic variant of Sangkima near Sangatta.

b_BOR_Muara_Wehea.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation; refers to the confluence of the Wehea River / Wehea forest territory in East Kalimantan.
b_BOR_Muara_Wehea.etymology_analysis: Combines the generic Malay locator prefix 'muara' ('river mouth/confluence') with 'Wehea', the name of the indigenous Dayak subgroup and protected rainforest in East Kutai.

b_BOR_Muara_Kaman.first_mention_attestation: The modern Malay name 'Muara Kaman' has no pre-867 CE attestation, though the site itself is famous for the c. 400 CE Sanskrit Yupa inscriptions of King Mulavarman.
b_BOR_Muara_Kaman.etymology_analysis: Malay 'muara' ('river mouth/confluence') + 'Kaman' (the Kaman tributary). While the Malay toponym is post-867 CE, the site yielded the c. 400 CE Sanskrit Yupa inscriptions of Kutai Martapura.

current_repo_state.name: Mûara Kaman
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Banjar Martapura dates to 1630 AD; resolves unambiguously via Option A to the 400 AD Mulavarman Sanskrit Yupa site at Muara Kaman (Mûara Kaman).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Mulavarman Yupa Sanskrit inscriptions at Muara Kaman (c. 400 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: The c. 400 CE Sanskrit Yupa inscriptions at Muara Kaman record the sacred sanctuary Vaprakesvara and King Mulavarman's dynasty.

b_BOR_Pemarangan.first_mention_attestation: Served as the 18th-century CE capital of the Kutai Kartanegara Sultanate until 1782 CE; no pre-867 CE attestation.

morphemes.translation: former royal seat of Kutai Kartanegara

b_BOR_Pemarangan.etymology_analysis: Pemarangan was an 18th-century CE royal center of the Sultanate of Kutai Kartanegara before Sultan Aji Muhammad Muslihuddin moved the capital to Tepian Pandan (Tenggarong) in 1782 CE.

b_BOR_Kutai_Loman.first_mention_attestation: Founded as the first capital of the Kutai Kartanegara kingdom around 1300 CE (with 'Tunjung Kute' attested in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama).

morphemes.translation: historic kingdom and region in East Kalimantan

b_BOR_Kutai_Loman.etymology_analysis: Malay 'Kutai Lama' ('Old Kutai', rendered 'Kutai Loman' in the mod key), the original c. 1300 CE capital of the Kutai Kartanegara kingdom before the capital moved upriver in 1732 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Kutai Loman
current_repo_state.b_origin: Kutai Loman (constituent holding of Mûara Kaman)

b_BOR_Bontang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Onderdistrict van Bontang under the Kutai Sultanate in 1920 CE; no pre-867 CE attestation.
b_BOR_Bontang.etymology_analysis: Local tradition interprets 'Bontang' as 'a group of visitors' (reflecting its origin as a coastal settlement of migrants under the Kutai Sultanate), though it was only formalized in 1920 CE.

b_BOR_Banjar.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the founding of the Sultanate of Banjar in 1526 CE (initially centered at Bandar Masih / Banjarmasin); no pre-867 CE attestation.
b_BOR_Banjar.etymology_analysis: Derived from Malay/Banjarese 'banjar' ('row' or 'settlement cluster'), applied to the 16th-century CE Sultanate of Banjar and its people in South Kalimantan.

current_repo_state.name: Bandschar
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Bandschar).

b_BOR_Katingan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Katingan' in the Old Javanese Nagarakretagama (1365 CE, Canto 13.2).

morphemes.translation: river and regional name in Central Kalimantan

b_BOR_Katingan.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Dayak name for the Katingan (Mendawai) River and its basin in Central Kalimantan, first recorded in writing in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama.

b_BOR_Kota_Raden.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE attestation; Kota Raden (Hulu/Hilir) is a modern/late-Banjar village in Amuntai Tengah, South Kalimantan.
b_BOR_Kota_Raden.etymology_analysis: Combines Malay 'kota' ('fort/town', from Sanskrit 'koṭṭa') with Javanese-Banjar noble title 'raden' ('prince'), reflecting Majapahit-era or Banjar Sultanate Javanese court influence.

b_BOR_Kapuas.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Kapuhas' in the Old Javanese Nagarakretagama (1365 CE, Canto 13.2).

morphemes.translation: name of the major river system in Borneo

b_BOR_Kapuas.etymology_analysis: Recorded as 'Kapuhas' in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama, referring to the Kapuas river system of Kalimantan (both the Kapuas Murung/Barito tributary in Central Kalimantan and the West Kalimantan Kapuas).

b_BOR_Sampit.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Sampit' in the Old Javanese Nagarakretagama (1365 CE, Canto 13.2).

morphemes.translation: river and port town in Central Kalimantan

b_BOR_Sampit.etymology_analysis: Indigenous toponym for the port and Mentaya/Sampit River basin in Central Kalimantan, first attested in writing in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama.

current_repo_state.name: Sampit
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Sampit).

b_BOR_Pembuang.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation; documented as a Banjar/Dutch colonial district (Distrik Pembuang) along the Seruyan/Pembuang River.

morphemes.translation: place of discarding / river channel name

b_BOR_Pembuang.etymology_analysis: Pembuang (also applied to the Seruyan River and Kuala Pembuang) is a Banjar/Malay riverine toponym in Central Kalimantan without pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_BOR_Sebangau.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation; Sebangau (Sabangau) is a modern river and peat-swamp national park name in Central Kalimantan.

morphemes.translation: blackwater river and peat-swamp forest name

b_BOR_Sebangau.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Central Kalimantan river and peat-swamp forest name between the Katingan and Kahayan rivers, lacking pre-867 CE written records.

b_BOR_Pasir.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Pasir' in the Old Javanese Nagarakretagama (1365 CE, Canto 14.1).

morphemes.translation: sand (also name of the Pasir River)

b_BOR_Pasir.etymology_analysis: Named after the Pasir River (formed by the confluence of the Seratei and Kendilo rivers) in East Kalimantan; first attested in writing in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama.

current_repo_state.name: Tabalung
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Tabalung).

b_BOR_Sepunang.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Tanjung Sepunang' in the 23 March 1904 CE border agreement between the Sultanates of Pasir and Kutai; no pre-867 CE attestation.
b_BOR_Sepunang.etymology_analysis: Refers to Tanjung Sepunang, a coastal cape on the Makassar Strait that served as the northern boundary marker of the Pasir Sultanate in 1904 CE.

b_BOR_Tunkaren.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation; likely a variant of Tungkaran (a village name in South Kalimantan).
b_BOR_Tunkaren.etymology_analysis: Unattested in pre-867 CE sources; possibly represents Tungkaran in South Kalimantan.

b_BOR_Taiao.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation; unattested in standard Indonesian/Malay historical gazetteers.
b_BOR_Taiao.etymology_analysis: No verified etymology or pre-867 CE historical attestation exists for 'Taiao' in southeastern Borneo.

current_repo_state.name: Taiau
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Taiau).

b_BOR_Kaburo.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation; unattested in standard historical sources for South Kalimantan.
b_BOR_Kaburo.etymology_analysis: No verified etymology or pre-867 CE historical attestation exists for 'Kaburo' in southeastern Borneo.

b_BOR_Laut.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation; Pulau Laut is documented in later Banjar Sultanate and Dutch colonial records.
b_BOR_Laut.etymology_analysis: From Malay/Indonesian 'laut' ('sea'), referring to Pulau Laut ('Sea Island') off the southeastern coast of South Kalimantan.

b_BOR_Sibu.first_mention_attestation: Founded as a Brooke outpost in 1862 CE and officially named 'Sibu' on 1 June 1873 CE (replacing the earlier name 'Maling'); no pre-867 CE attestation.
b_BOR_Sibu.etymology_analysis: Named after the 'sibau' (wild rambutan) fruit trees abundant in the area. Known as 'Maling' until 1873 CE, Sibu was established by Rajah James Brooke in 1862 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Iban
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Iban).

b_BOR_Melano.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Malano' in the Old Javanese Nagarakretagama (1365 CE, Canto 14.1); no pre-867 CE written attestation.

morphemes.translation: coastal Sarawak region and ethnic group

b_BOR_Melano.etymology_analysis: Historical regional and ethnic name ('Malano' in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama) for the Melanau people and coastal kingdom of central Sarawak.

b_BOR_Bintulu.first_mention_attestation: Documented as a fishing village ceded by the Sultanate of Brunei to Rajah James Brooke in 1861 CE; no pre-867 CE attestation.

morphemes.translation: retrieving heads cast into the river (traditional etymology)

b_BOR_Bintulu.etymology_analysis: Traditional local etymology derives Bintulu from 'mëntu ulu' ('picking up heads' from the river), though its written history begins with its 1861 CE cession from Brunei to Sarawak.

b_BOR_Miri.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1910 CE when the first oil well was drilled by Shell; no pre-867 CE written attestation.

morphemes.translation: indigenous minority ethnic group of northern Sarawak

b_BOR_Miri.etymology_analysis: Named after the indigenous 'Jati Miriek' (Miri) minority group of the area; the modern town was founded in 1910 CE around oil discovery.

b_BOR_Long.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation; 'Long' is a Kayan/Kenyah generic toponymic prefix meaning 'river mouth' or 'confluence'.
b_BOR_Long.etymology_analysis: In Kayan, Kenyah, and other Orang Ulu languages of interior Sarawak and Kalimantan, 'long' is a generic geographical term for a river mouth or confluence.

current_repo_state.name: Radschang
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Radschang).

b_BOR_Rajang_Atas.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation; 'Rajang Atas' ('Upper Rajang') is a modern Malay geographical designation.
b_BOR_Rajang_Atas.etymology_analysis: Combines 'Rajang' (Malaysia's longest river) with the Malay directional modifier 'atas' ('upper'). No pre-867 CE written attestation exists.

b_BOR_Santubong.first_mention_attestation: While the Santubong archaeological site yielded Tang and Song Chinese ceramics (8th–13th centuries CE), the name 'Santubong' itself has no contemporary pre-867 CE written attestation.

morphemes.translation: coastal mountain and archaeological port in Sarawak

b_BOR_Santubong.etymology_analysis: Named after Mount Santubong at the mouth of the Sarawak River. Archaeological excavations show iron-smelting and trade from the 8th–13th centuries CE, but the toponym itself is unattested in pre-867 CE texts.

b_BOR_Sedu.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Sedu' ('ri sedu') in the Old Javanese Nagarakretagama (1365 CE, Canto 14.1).

morphemes.translation: medieval Bornean polity (identified with Sadong or Seduan in Sarawak)

b_BOR_Sedu.etymology_analysis: Mentioned as 'Sedu' in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama among Majapahit's Bornean dependencies, generally identified with Sadong or Seduan in Sarawak.

b_BOR_Sigalang.first_mention_attestation: Known from Sarikei oral history as a settlement existing roughly 300 years ago (c. 17th–18th century CE); no pre-867 CE attestation.
b_BOR_Sigalang.eponym_details: Named after Sigalang, a revered local headman of the early settlement between the Sarikei and Nyelong rivers (c. 17th–18th century CE).

morphemes.translation: personal name of the community headman
