b_BOR_Sigalang.etymology_analysis: Named after a fair and just headman, Sigalang, whose community was the earliest recorded settlement in the Sarikei area of Sarawak around 300 years ago.

b_BOR_Kanowit.first_mention_attestation: Documented in Sarawak Brooke records from 1849–1851 CE (when Fort Betong / Fort Kanowit was built); no pre-867 CE attestation.

morphemes.translation: indigenous ethnic group and river name

b_BOR_Kanowit.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Kanowit ethnic group (culturally related to the Melanau) who settled along the Kanowit River, a tributary of the Rajang in Sarawak.

b_BOR_Tanah_Taman.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation; refers to the homeland of the Dayak Taman (Banuaka') people in Kapuas Hulu, West Kalimantan.

morphemes.translation: Dayak Taman ethnic group of Kapuas Hulu

b_BOR_Tanah_Taman.etymology_analysis: Malay 'tanah' ('land') + 'Taman' (the Dayak Taman / Banuaka' people of the upper Kapuas basin in West Kalimantan).

current_repo_state.name: Tanah Taman
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Tanah Taman).

b_BOR_Malu.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation; likely a variant of Mulu (Mount Mulu, Sarawak) or an unattested minor toponym.
b_BOR_Malu.etymology_analysis: No historical attestation exists for 'Malu' in interior Borneo; if representing Mount Mulu in Sarawak, it was first surveyed in the mid-20th century CE.

b_BOR_Sambas.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Sambas' in the Old Javanese Nagarakretagama (1365 CE, Canto 13.2); the 9th-century CE Sambas Treasure is an archaeological find without an inscribed toponym.

morphemes.translation: river and historic sultanate in West Kalimantan

b_BOR_Sambas.etymology_analysis: Sambas is a historic coastal kingdom and sultanate (established 1609 CE) in West Kalimantan, first attested in writing as 'Sambas' in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama.

current_repo_state.name: Sambas
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Sambas).

b_BOR_Landak.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Landa' in the Old Javanese Kakawin Nagarakretagama (1365 CE) among Majapahit's claimed tributaries in Borneo (Nusa Tanjungnagara).
b_BOR_Landak.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Malay/Dayak noun 'landak' (porcupine), applied to the Landak River in West Kalimantan and the polity established along its banks.

b_BOR_Mempawah.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary pre-modern epigraphic or chronicle date is established; local traditions trace the Mempawah polity to post-14th-century Malay-Dayak settlements and the 17th–18th-century Panembahan Mempawah.
b_BOR_Mempawah.etymology_analysis: Named after the Mempawah River in West Kalimantan, itself traditionally derived from 'mempauh', the local Malay name for a tree growing along its upper reaches.

b_BOR_Sanggau.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary pre-modern epigraphic attestation; local tradition dates the founding of the Sanggau Kingdom to 1310 CE, with written records appearing in the early modern era.
b_BOR_Sanggau.etymology_analysis: According to local West Kalimantan tradition, the name Sanggau derives from a plant growing along the Sekayam River where the early settlement was established.

b_BOR_Sintang.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE attestation; Sintang enters written records in later Bornean and Javanese-Malay historical traditions (such as the Hikayat Banjar, compiled by 1663 CE, and early modern Sultanate records).

morphemes.translation: facing or opposite (the confluence of the Kapuas and Melawi rivers)

b_BOR_Sintang.etymology_analysis: Toponym of West Kalimantan at the confluence of the Kapuas and Melawi rivers, traditionally linked to 'senentang' (facing/opposite the river junction).

current_repo_state.name: Sintang
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Sintang).

b_BOR_Teinangga.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical records; appears to be a modder-coined or corrupted West Kalimantan toponym.
b_BOR_Teinangga.etymology_analysis: No historical settlement named Teinangga is documented in West Kalimantan; the final element may reflect 'nanga' (river confluence), common in Sintang and Kapuas Hulu toponymy.

b_BOR_Sukadana.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; historic coastal port and royal capital of the Tanjungpura / Sukadana kingdom in West Kalimantan, emerging in the 15th–16th centuries CE and documented in the Hikayat Banjar and early 17th-century European trade records
b_BOR_Sukadana.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit-Malay compound Sukadana ('joyful gift / place of generous wealth'), naming the historic diamond-trading port and successor capital of the Kingdom of Tanjungpura in West Kalimantan, Borneo.

b_BOR_Samedang.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Samedang' in Canto 14 of the Old Javanese Kakawin Nagarakretagama (1365 CE) among Majapahit's claimed dependencies in Borneo.
b_BOR_Samedang.etymology_analysis: Recorded in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama as one of the Bornean polities under Tanjungnagara; its exact local linguistic root is uncertain.

b_BOR_Sekadao.first_mention_attestation: No pre-modern epigraphic date; local historical accounts place the formation of the Sekadau polity around c. 1600 CE.

morphemes.translation: local tree species growing along the river

b_BOR_Sekadao.etymology_analysis: Named after the Sekadau River in West Kalimantan, which according to local tradition took its name from a species of tree growing along its banks.

b_BOR_Kota_Waringin.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Kuta Waringin' in the Old Javanese Kakawin Nagarakretagama (1365 CE) among Majapahit's claimed dependencies in Borneo.
b_BOR_Kota_Waringin.etymology_analysis: Compound of 'kuta/kota' (fortified town, from Sanskrit 'kotta') and 'waringin' (banyan tree), meaning 'banyan-tree fort/town'.

current_repo_state.name: Waringin
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Waringin).

b_BOR_Warau.first_mention_attestation: No confirmed pre-modern historical attestation in Bornean or Javanese sources for a settlement named Warau.
b_BOR_Warau.etymology_analysis: Unattested local or mod-adapted name in Central Kalimantan; possibly a variant or misreading of a regional Bornean name such as Barau/Berau.

b_BOR_Seruyan.first_mention_attestation: No pre-modern epigraphic attestation; the Seruyan river basin (as Pembuang) appears in the 17th-century Hikayat Banjar (1663 CE), and Seruyan Regency was formally established in 2002 CE.
b_BOR_Seruyan.etymology_analysis: Named after the Seruyan River in Central Kalimantan.

b_IDO_Bedulu.first_mention_attestation: 1365 CE (explicitly attested as Bedahulu in Canto 14, verse 3 of Mpu Prapanca's Old Javanese Kakawin Nagarakretagama, naming the royal seat of Bali alongside Lwa Gajah)
b_IDO_Bedulu.etymology_analysis: Contracted from Old Balinese/Old Javanese Bedahulu (literally 'changed/different head', linked in Balinese folklore to the pig-headed king Maya Denawa / Sri Astasura, or 'upstream seat'), capital of the pre-Majapahit Balinese kingdom in Gianyar, attested in 1365 CE.

b_IDO_Buleleng.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the mid-17th century (c. 1660 CE) with the establishment of the Kingdom of Buleleng by I Gusti Anglurah Panji Sakti in northern Bali.

morphemes.translation: jagung gembal / local maize variety (traditional etymology)

b_IDO_Buleleng.etymology_analysis: Northern Balinese toponym associated with the 17th-century Kingdom of Buleleng; local tradition derives it from 'buleleng', a variety of maize/grain.

b_IDO_Jembrana.first_mention_attestation: Recorded in European accounts by Dutch explorer Cornelis de Houtman in 1597 CE, and later as one of the nine minor kingdoms of Bali in the 17th–18th centuries.
b_IDO_Jembrana.etymology_analysis: Traditionally derived from Old Javanese/Balinese 'jimbar' (wide) + 'wana' (forest), referring to the expansive forests of western Bali.

b_IDO_Bima.first_mention_attestation: 1365 CE (explicitly attested as Bhīma / Bima in Canto 14, verse 3 of Mpu Prapanca's Old Javanese Kakawin Nagarakretagama as a Majapahit-era polity on eastern Sumbawa)

morphemes.translation: the formidable/awesome one (name of the Mahabharata Pandava hero adopted into Sumbawan royal toponymy)

b_IDO_Bima.etymology_analysis: Exonym and royal polity name for eastern Sumbawa (locally known as Mbojo), derived from the Mahabharata hero Bhīma via Javanese Hindu-Buddhist cultural influence; first epigraphically/literarily attested in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama.

b_IDO_Lombok.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Lombok Mirah' in Canto 14 of the Old Javanese Kakawin Nagarakretagama (1365 CE).
b_IDO_Lombok.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Javanese/Sasak 'lomboq' meaning 'straight' or 'honest' (unrelated to the Javanese word for chili pepper).

b_IDO_Taliwang.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Taliwang' in Canto 14 of the Old Javanese Kakawin Nagarakretagama (1365 CE) among polities east of Java.

morphemes.translation: historical polity name on western Sumbawa

b_IDO_Taliwang.etymology_analysis: Toponym of western Sumbawa recorded in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama and later a vassal kingdom (Kedatuan Taliwang) under Sumbawa.

b_JAV_Sampang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; while Madura Island is attested in 1255 and 1365 CE, Sampang specifically enters written records in post-Majapahit Madurese and Javanese babad chronicles (16th–17th centuries CE)
b_JAV_Sampang.etymology_analysis: Madurese town and historic regency on the south-central coast of Madura Island, locally explained from Madurese e'sempange ('place passed through / waypoint') in folklore surrounding Prince Jokotole.

b_JAV_Sumenep.first_mention_attestation: Established as the Duchy of Sumenep ('Sungeneb') on 31 October 1269 CE under Arya Wiraraja during the Singhasari period.
b_JAV_Sumenep.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Javanese 'Sungeneb' (also rendered 'Songenep'), meaning 'calm/quiet valley'.

b_JAV_Kangean.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE or pre-modern epigraphic attestation; the Kangean Islands appear in later Madurese and Dutch colonial geographic records.

morphemes.translation: island group name east of Madura

b_JAV_Kangean.etymology_analysis: Island and archipelago name in the Java Sea east of Madura, inhabited by the Madurese-related Kangean people.

b_JAV_Kahuripan.first_mention_attestation: 1037 CE (explicitly attested in King Airlangga's 959 Saka / 1037 CE Kamalagyan inscription documenting the capital at Kahuripan, and in the 1041 CE Pucangan / Calcutta Stone inscription)
b_JAV_Kahuripan.etymology_analysis: Old Javanese Kahuripan ('life' or 'livelihood', from ka-...-an + hurip 'to live'), founded by King Airlangga in East Java as the restored Mataram/Medang capital in the Brantas delta, attested epigraphically in 1037 CE.

b_JAV_Hujung_Galuh.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Kelagen inscription (1037 CE) of King Airlangga, which records the development of the port of Hujung Galuh at the Brantas River estuary.
b_JAV_Hujung_Galuh.etymology_analysis: Old Javanese compound 'hujung' (point/cape) + 'galuh' (gemstone), referring to the major 11th–14th-century river-mouth port near modern Surabaya.

b_JAV_Daha.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Dahanapura' in the Pamwatan inscription (1042 CE) issued by King Airlangga.
b_JAV_Daha.etymology_analysis: Abbreviation of Sanskrit 'Dahanapura' ('city of fire', from 'dahana' fire + 'pura' city), the capital of the Kediri Kingdom.

b_JAV_Tamwlang.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 929 CE inscriptions of King Mpu Sindok (who moved the Mataram/Medang court from Central Java to Tamwlang in East Java).

morphemes.translation: ancient settlement name in Jombang (modern Tembelang)

b_JAV_Tamwlang.etymology_analysis: Old Javanese toponym in East Java (modern Tembelang, Jombang Regency) where Mpu Sindok first established his East Javanese court in 929 CE.

b_JAV_Kambang_Putih.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE epigraphic attestation; known in East Javanese historical tradition as an earlier name for the port of Tuban (attested from the Singhasari/Majapahit era, 13th–14th century CE).
b_JAV_Kambang_Putih.etymology_analysis: Old Javanese/Javanese compound meaning 'white flower' (or 'white float'), the historical name associated with the northern Javanese port of Tuban.

b_JAV_Anjukladang.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Anjuk Ladang (Candi Lor) inscription dated 859 Saka (937 CE) issued by King Mpu Sindok.
b_JAV_Anjukladang.etymology_analysis: Old Javanese toponym meaning 'high field' or 'field of victory', the ancestor of the modern name Nganjuk.

b_JAV_Dieng.first_mention_attestation: 809 CE (attested as Old Javanese Dihyang / Di Hyang in the 731 Saka / 809 CE Dieng inscription and in the 861 CE Gunung Wule inscription referencing bhaṭāra i dihyang; Hindu candi temple construction on the plateau dates from the late 7th–8th century CE)
b_JAV_Dieng.etymology_analysis: Modern contraction of Old Javanese Dihyang / Di Hyang ('abode of the gods / place of the ancestors'), naming the sacred volcanic highland plateau in Central Java that hosts Java's oldest surviving Hindu stone temples and Old Javanese inscriptions from 809 CE onward.

b_JAV_Poh_Pitu.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Mantyasih inscription (11 April 907 CE) of King Balitung ('ri mḍaṅ, ri poḥ pitu').
b_JAV_Poh_Pitu.etymology_analysis: Old Javanese compound meaning 'seven mangoes', a royal court/capital site of the Mataram Kingdom under Balitung and his successors.

b_JAV_Lwaram.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Pucangan (Calcutta Stone) inscription (1041 CE), which records King Wurawari of Lwaram's attack on Wwatan in 1016–1017 CE.

morphemes.translation: ancient polity/place name (identified with Ngloram in Blora)

b_JAV_Lwaram.etymology_analysis: Old Javanese toponym of a vassal polity under Mataram, generally identified with modern Ngloram near Cepu, Blora Regency, Central Java.

b_JAV_Kuwu.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE epigraphic attestation; Kuwu (associated with Bledug Kuwu in Grobogan) appears in later Javanese legendary and colonial records.
b_JAV_Kuwu.etymology_analysis: From Old Javanese/Javanese 'kuwu' (village headman/chief), applied to the village of Kuwu in Grobogan Regency, Central Java.

b_JAV_Keling.first_mention_attestation: 640 CE (Javanese form of Kalingga, attested in Tang dynasty annals Jiu Tangshu and Xin Tangshu as Heling / Ho-ling 訶陵 sending embassies from 640 CE onward, and recorded by Yijing in 671 CE)

morphemes.translation: named after the Kalinga region of eastern India (modern Odisha)

b_JAV_Keling.etymology_analysis: Javanese form of Sanskrit Kaliṅga (from Kalinga in eastern India), naming the early Indianized kingdom of Kalingga / Keling on north-central Java (modern Jepara/Keling area, later also associated with Kediri), attested in Tang Chinese annals as Heling (訶陵) from 640 CE.

b_JAV_Blambangan.first_mention_attestation: 1365 CE (attested as Balambangan / Blambangan in the Old Javanese Kakawin Nagarakretagama of 1365 CE and in the Pararaton, naming easternmost Java)
b_JAV_Blambangan.etymology_analysis: Old Javanese toponym (Balambangan) for the easternmost Hindu-Javanese kingdom in the Banyuwangi/Oosthoek peninsula of East Java, attested in Mpu Prapanca's 1365 CE Nagarakretagama.

b_JAV_Situbondo.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE attestation; Situbondo emerged in the post-Majapahit/early modern period (replacing Panarukan as the regency seat).
b_JAV_Situbondo.etymology_analysis: Derived in local etymology from Javanese 'siti bondo' ('binding land', attracting settlers to stay), or alternatively linked in folklore to Prince Aryo Gajah Situbondo.

b_JAV_Pasuruhan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Pasuruhan' in Canto 35 of the Old Javanese Kakawin Nagarakretagama (1365 CE).
b_JAV_Pasuruhan.etymology_analysis: Old Javanese locative formation 'pa-suruh-an' meaning 'place of betel leaves', attested in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama.

b_JAV_Tumapel.first_mention_attestation: Recorded as the seat of Ken Arok (1222 CE) in the Pararaton and Nagarakretagama (1365 CE) as the predecessor/province of Singhasari in the Malang valley.

morphemes.translation: East Javanese polity name in the Malang highlands

b_JAV_Tumapel.etymology_analysis: Old Javanese name of the Malang highland polity prior to and alongside Singhasari (13th century CE).

b_JAV_Mataram.first_mention_attestation: Earliest explicit epigraphic occurrences of i bhūmi i mātaram / Rakai Mataram appear post-867 CE in the Wuatan Tija inscription (880 CE) and the Mantyasih and Rukam inscriptions (907 CE), which retrospectively title King Sanjaya (of the 732 CE Sanskrit Canggal inscription) as Rakai Mataram; neither Canggal (732 CE) nor Shivagrha (856 CE) contains the name Mātarām.
b_JAV_Mataram.etymology_analysis: Old Javanese polity/region name Mātarām (Sanskritized Mātaram, traditionally glossed via 'mother' or local Javanese toponymy). While King Sanjaya's 732 CE Canggal inscription records Yavadvīpa and Kuñjarakuñjadeśa, the toponym Mātarām itself is first epigraphically attested post-867 CE in Wuatan Tija (880 CE) and Mantyasih/Rukam (907 CE).

b_JAV_Mamrati.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Mamratipura' in the Shivagrha inscription dated 778 Saka (856 CE) under Rakai Pikatan.

morphemes.translation: royal court location in the Kedu Plain

b_JAV_Mamrati.etymology_analysis: Old Javanese royal court name (also 'Mamratipura') in Central Java's Kedu Plain, attested in the 856 CE Shivagrha inscription.

b_JAV_Borobodur.first_mention_attestation: Although the monument was constructed c. 780–833 CE, the name 'Borobudur' is first attested in late form as 'Budur' in the Kakawin Nagarakretagama (1365 CE) and fully as 'Bóro Bódo' by Raffles (1817 CE).

morphemes.translation: nearby village name (or mountain / palm tree)

b_JAV_Borobodur.etymology_analysis: Commonly derived from 'bara/boro' (from Sanskrit 'vihāra', monastery) + 'Budur' (the nearby village name, attested in 1365 CE).

b_JAV_Wwatan.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Pucangan (Calcutta Stone) inscription (1041 CE), which records the destruction of Dharmawangsa's capital at Wwatan in 1016–1017 CE.

morphemes.translation: audience hall, royal court, or wooden beam

b_JAV_Wwatan.etymology_analysis: Old Javanese toponym (often identified with Wotan Mas near Madiun or Mojokerto) that served as Dharmawangsa's capital in East Java.

b_JAV_Bagaluhan.first_mention_attestation: The Bagelen region is first attested in the Kayu Ara Hiwang inscription (5 October 901 CE) in Purworejo, Central Java.
b_JAV_Bagaluhan.etymology_analysis: Historical Old Javanese form corresponding to Bagelen in Purworejo, Central Java, attested from the early 10th century CE.

b_JAV_Kampak.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Kampak' in the Kampak inscription (c. 929–930 CE, dated by official titles to 851–852 Saka) of King Mpu Sindok.

morphemes.translation: axe or historical village name in Trenggalek

b_JAV_Kampak.etymology_analysis: Old Javanese settlement name in Trenggalek, East Java, granted sima status by Mpu Sindok in the c. 929–930 CE Kampak inscription.

b_JAV_Cimanuk.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Chemano' (Chi Manuk / Cimanuk) in Tomé Pires' Suma Oriental (1512–1515 CE) as the easternmost port of the Sunda Kingdom.
b_JAV_Cimanuk.etymology_analysis: Sundanese hydronym meaning 'bird river' (from 'ci' water/river + 'manuk' bird). The input's 'Tschîmanuch' is a Germanized spelling.

b_JAV_Batujaya.first_mention_attestation: Although the Batujaya temple complex dates archaeologically to the 2nd–12th centuries CE (Tarumanagara era), the modern village name 'Batujaya' has no pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_JAV_Batujaya.etymology_analysis: Modern Indonesian/Sundanese compound meaning 'victorious stone', applied to the Karawang village hosting the ancient Tarumanagara-era brick temple complex.

b_JAV_Bojang_Menje.first_mention_attestation: Although the Candi Bojongmenje temple ruins date archaeologically to the 7th–8th centuries CE, the hamlet name 'Bojongmenje' has no pre-867 CE written attestation.

morphemes.translation: bend in a river or promontory

b_JAV_Bojang_Menje.etymology_analysis: Sundanese hamlet toponym in Rancaekek, Bandung Regency ('bojong' river bend + 'menje'), where 7th-century Hindu temple ruins were discovered in 2002 CE.

b_JAV_Kawali.first_mention_attestation: c. 1350 CE (explicitly attested as Kawali in the 14th-century CE Old Sundanese Kawali / Astana Gede inscriptions in Ciamis, West Java, commemorating King Niskala Wastu Kancana's capital)

morphemes.translation: cauldron, wide basin, or frying pan (referring to the valley basin or royal citadel)

b_JAV_Kawali.etymology_analysis: Old Sundanese toponym of the Astana Gede / Kawali royal capital of the Sunda-Galuh kingdom in Ciamis, West Java, epigraphically attested in the 14th-century Kawali stone inscriptions (c. 1350–1400 CE).

b_JAV_Cirebon.first_mention_attestation: Established as Caruban in 1445 CE (declaring independence in 1482 CE) per Cirebon chronicles, and attested as 'Charabaon' / 'Cheribon' in 16th-century Portuguese accounts (Tomé Pires, 1512–1515 CE).
b_JAV_Cirebon.etymology_analysis: Traditionally derived either from Sundanese 'ci-rebon' ('shrimp water', from shrimp paste production) or Javanese/Sundanese 'caruban' ('mixture', reflecting its multi-ethnic port population).

b_JAV_Pangandaran.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE attestation; Pangandaran developed as a coastal fishing settlement in southeastern West Java in the early modern/colonial era.
b_JAV_Pangandaran.etymology_analysis: Sundanese coastal toponym on the southern coast of West Java, traditionally associated with a landing or anchoring place for fishermen.

b_JAV_Purwokerto.first_mention_attestation: Established as an administrative center (originally Purwakerta) on 6 October 1832 CE under Regent Raden Adipati Mertadiredja II.
b_JAV_Purwokerto.etymology_analysis: From Javanese 'Purwakerta' ('first/beginning of prosperity' or 'built at the beginning', from Sanskrit 'pūrva' + 'kṛta').

b_JAV_Limbangan.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE attestation; Balubur Limbangan is documented as a Priangan regency in the Mataram and Dutch colonial periods (17th–19th centuries CE, prior to the 1813/1821 move to Garut).
b_JAV_Limbangan.etymology_analysis: Sundanese toponym meaning 'place of panning/washing' (in Garut Regency, West Java).

b_JAV_Pakuan_Pajajaran.first_mention_attestation: 1533 CE (explicitly attested as Pakwan Pajajaran in the 1455 Saka / 1533 CE Old Sundanese Batutulis inscription in Bogor, and referenced in late-15th/early-16th-century Sundanese manuscripts such as Bujangga Manik and Carita Parahyangan)

morphemes.translation: royal palace/court, or place of paku trees/ferns
parallel, lined up (referring to parallel rivers Ciliwung and Cisadane or aligned pakujajar trees)

b_JAV_Pakuan_Pajajaran.etymology_analysis: Old Sundanese royal capital name (modern Bogor, West Java) of the Sunda Kingdom, combining pakwan ('royal court' or 'place of paku') with pajajaran ('parallel/aligned'); commemorated in King Surawisesa's 1533 CE Batutulis inscription.

b_JAV_Banten.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Bantam' (Banten) in Tomé Pires' Suma Oriental (1512–1515 CE) as one of the major ports of the Sunda Kingdom.

morphemes.translation: offering or sacred tribute (also linked to a river name)

b_JAV_Banten.etymology_analysis: From Sundanese/Javanese 'Wahanten' / 'Banten', a major port city in westernmost Java that became the seat of the Banten Sultanate in the 16th century.

b_JAV_Tangaram.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Tamgaram' (Tangaram) in Tomé Pires' Suma Oriental (1512–1515 CE) among the ports of the Kingdom of Sunda.

morphemes.translation: boundary marker or coastal port name

b_JAV_Tangaram.etymology_analysis: Sundanese port toponym on the Cisadane River west of Jakarta, recorded by Tomé Pires in 1512–1515 CE as 'Tamgaram'.

b_JAV_Tugu.first_mention_attestation: Although the 5th-century CE Tarumanagara 'Tugu inscription' was discovered there, the village name 'Tugu' itself dates to the early modern/colonial era (after the inscribed stone monument/tugu or the Portuguese-descended Mardijkers).
b_JAV_Tugu.etymology_analysis: Indonesian/Javanese 'tugu' (monument/pillar), referring to the 5th-century Purnavarman inscription stone found in the area (or alternatively from 'Por-Tugu-ese' Mardijkers settled there in the 17th century).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Tugu inscription of King Purnavarman of Tarumanagara (c. 5th century CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Kampung Tugu is the findspot of the 5th-century CE Sanskrit Tugu inscription of Tarumanagara, recording King Purnavarman's excavation of the Candrabhāgā and Gomatī channels prior to the modern village name Tugu.

b_JAV_Cicatih.first_mention_attestation: While the Sanghyang Tapak inscription (1030 CE) was found on the banks of the Cicatih River, the river name 'Cicatih' itself has no pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_JAV_Cicatih.etymology_analysis: Sundanese hydronym in Sukabumi, West Java, formed with the river prefix 'ci-' (water/river) + 'catih'.

b_JAV_Ujung_Kulon.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation; Ujung Kulon appears in early modern and colonial geographic records as the westernmost peninsula of Java.
b_JAV_Ujung_Kulon.etymology_analysis: Compound meaning 'western tip' or 'western cape', describing the westernmost peninsula of Java.
